speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: KING OF BELGIUM NOT TO VISIT CANADA.
speechtext:
Several days ago I was asked whether an invitation had been extended to Their Majesties the King and Queen of Belgium to visit Canada, and if so, whether it had been

accepted. I was not able to say at the time whether the invitation had been accepted or not. An invitation has been sent, and Their Majesties regret very much that owing to the shortness of time at their disposal on this continent they will not be able to visit Canada as they would very much have liked to do.

speechtext:
I notice on page 15 of the blue-book a cablegram from the Prime Minister referring to the Grand Trunk. I have quoted it on a former occasion. The substance of what he says is that there should be some definite information in connection with the Grand Trunk system before any further negotiations for its purchase take place; that the Government have nothing except the Drayton-Acworth report. Has the minister any later report on the condition of the Grand Trunk as to its roadbed, locomotives, freight and passenger cars and everything belonging to the system? To give the Prime Minister's exact words:
It is most unwise and undesirable for a government without the report of a commission or Board of Arbitration or a vote of parliament to undertake a large annual payment which would represent the capitalization of eighty or a hundred million dollars. The offer already made is based on the DTayton-Acworth report which affords a sufficient foundation for Government's proposal. If we go beyond the bounds of that report we have no certain guide as to what we should propose, etc.
Now, this report is getting somewhat old. The road has been operated continuously. Evidently the company have all along contemplated the desirability of selling, and naturally, like other people, they would not lavish expenditures on the road when they were trying to get clear of it. I think the people would like to know exactly how the matter stands now. Has the minister any report on the condition of the rolling stock and everything else that we are taking over?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister evidently differs from the Minister of Finance ('Sir Henry Drayton). It is a well-known fact that during the war and for the last few years the Grand Trunk has not spent a very large amount on the rolling stock and equipment of the line. In 1916 the Minister of Finance, who was then president of the commission appointed by the Government to inquire into the matter, made this statement:
Further, the Grand Trunk Railway has not been and is not being- adequately maintained No depreciation fund has been created for equipment. Mr. Chamberlin's view, as shown by his evidence, is that 5 per cent on the cost of the equipment ought to be annually charged under this head. He says :-
" Take engines and cars, they are either
worn out or out of date in twenty years."
This item, according to his evidence, would have required an annual sum of $2,750,000. He also states:-
"If we had $25,000,000 now, It would put
us in fine shape."
The Vice-President of operation, Mr. Kelley,-
The same gentleman whom the minister quotes

has direct responsibility for the plant. On Mr. Chamberlin's evidence being put to him he agreed with it.
So that Mr. Kelley, the president of the company, whom the Minister of Railways quotes as an authority in regard to the condition of the road, in 1916 agreed with Mr. Chamberlin in the statement that it would take $25,000,000 to "put us in fine shape." The Minister of Finance at that time stated in his report that the Grand Trunk Railway had not -been and was not being adequately maintained. Moreover, he says:
On the single item of " rails " the " cash expenditure required to restore normal conditions "-
Not for purposes of extension or improvement, but purely and simply to restore normal conditions.
-is reported as $5,312,142. The cost of restoring 'ballast to normal conditions is reported as $2,434,000.
With reference to the deferred renewals in Canada amounting to over $6,000,000, it appears that they have accumulated during eleven years, 1906-16. During this period, in spite of the requirements of the property, and the claims of public safety, $36,0-00y0'0'0 were paid out in dividends.
Summarizing the evidence given by Mr. Chamberlin and Mr. Kelley, the minister in his report states:
The $21,000,000 dealt with above represent the money which The responsible officers of the company estimate to be required to put the existing plant into good normal condition. This is a revenue liability. But the existing plant is quite inadequate for existing traffic and requires large additions, for which new capital must be raised. The estimates of necessary capital expenditure submitted to us are as follows:
Requirements for rolling stock,
shops and. machinery	 $26,150,000
Requirements for automatic -block signals (main line in Canada
only)	  3,533,000
Requirements for installing rock
ballast crushing plant	 467,500
Total	!	 $30,150,500
Putting together revenue and capital expenditure, we find that the Grand Trunk railway, in the opinion of its own officers, requires over

$51,000,000 spent upon it to put it in a position to meet the requirements of its to-day's business. We see no reason to expect that under existing conditions this necessary money will be ' provided.
The opinion of the Minister of Railways is thus in direct conflict with the studied statement of the Minister of Finance, who made a full investigation of the physical condition of the road and its equipment in 1916, when he said that it would require $51,000,000 merely to put the road in normal condition. The Minister of Railways asks Parliament to support .this Bill, which has for its object the purchasing of the Grand Trunk-if it can be termed a purchase- and does not know himself what the present physical condition of the road is.
He tells us that he has nothing else in his hands than the annual reports sent to the railway department by the railway company; he tells us that he has nothing but the letter from Mr. Kelley who, in 1916, made several startling statements, and he tells us that he has no further knowledge than the knowledge that he acquired by travelling on some sections of the road. I submit that is not the information that the House is entitled to receive and I do not think the Government is justified in recommending such legislation before it has gone fully into the physical condition of the road and has further knowledge to acquaint Parliament with.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Notwithstanding all that the hon. member has read in the Drayton-Acworth report about the condition of the road at that time, Sir Henry Drayton having taken all the evidence, here is what he recommends, page 87:
that a new public authority, a Board of Trustees be incorporated by Act of Parliament as the "Dominion Railway Company''-.
We have done that in regard to the Canadian National railways-

and that the Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific be transferred to this body.
On the next page, 88, section 40 of the Drayton-Acworth report, the commissioners
say:	^	-
We recommend that the entire share capital of the Grand Trunk, guaranteed, preference and ordinary, be surrendered to the trustees in exchange for an annuity based on a moderate out substantial proportion of $3,600,000, the average sum paid as dividend in the last ten years; and that this annuity should increase by forty or fifty per cent after the first seven years.
That is the recommendation of the present Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton). I go farther and say that now that he is a

member of the Government he is not only as strong to-day as he was then hut much stronger in the 'belief that we should acquire that road and make it a part of the Canadian National Railways system. On these terms he is a 'party to it and very strongly in favour of it. Possibly the equipment might not have been in as good condition at that time as it is to-day. Barge sums have been expended. There is a statement on Hansard, page 1145, showing that large sums have been expended from that date up to the present time on the improvement of the equipment. Therefore I submit that the Drayton-Acworth commission having recommended that we acquire the road and the report of President Kelley at the present time stating what the equipment is, we are justified in taking it over, believing that the equipment is in good shape, and that we are also justified in carrying out the suggestion of the commission that we take over the road on the lines recommended by them.

speechtext: Taking the five stocks. They say: Take the five stocks and we will recommend that we pay a lump sum and then let the directors divide it amongst these stocks as they deem proper. speechtext: No, we found that it was not a matter for the directors until they received their dividend of $2,500,000. It was shown very clearly to the Minister of Finance, as to every one else, that the guaranteed stockholders had first claim on the capital in liquidation and had first claim on the revenues during operation; consequently anything paid in respect to the five stocks had to be applied to the guaranteed stock any way until the claims of the holders of this stock were satisfied. These are the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth report, read.in the light of the exact facts, and this is just what we are doing.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not agree with the minister at all. The Drayton-Acworth report-which is the confession of faith of the Government, and upon which they base their whole operations and say everything they are now doing depends-tells them in section 41, which the minister was pleased to refer to, to do one thing and they are doing another thing entirely. I do not think it can be understood by any hon. gentleman in this House that taking a substantial, or moderate proportion of $3,600,000 and paying that over annually to the directors for the first seven years, and telling them:	" Divide that between your stocks
just as you please, it is none of our business, you can put it on any stock you like, but we are only obligating ourselves to pay you a moderate or substantial proportion of $3,600,000," is what the Government are doing, but it is the recommendation in the Drayton-Acworth report. Instead of doing that we take four of five stocks, which the Government say should come in, and we leave another stock out and we agree to pay upon the one which we leave out $2,500,000 a year-almost as much on the one stock .as the Drayton-Acworth report says we should put upon the whole. The Government say: "But $2,500,000 is a substantial amount of $3,600,000." It is a substantial amount. That is all the Drayton-Acworth report expects us to pay altogether but we pay that sum upon one set of stocks and we take the responsibility for what the arbitration may say we will have to pay upon the balance. I am not as much criticising that as I am criticising this: The Government cannot blow hot and blow cold upon this thing. They cannot take shelter behind the Drayton-Acworth report and at the same time fail to do what the Drayton-Acworth report recommends. That is the position I take.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
On October 16, I made in this House a detailed statement of all the obligations and charges of the Grand Trunk railway. That statement was based on the Grand Trunk Railway Company's annual report for 1917, Moodie's Analysis of Steam Railroad Investments, information contained in Hansard, and railway statistics and it is set forth at pages 1145, 1146, 1147 and 1148-49 of Hansard. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. H. H. McLean) repeated the figures from the same statement and the Minister of Railways declared they were not correct. He asked in what respect they were incorrect, and the minister artistically declared, " It is not so at all. I do not agree with it at all."
Since then my figures have not been challenged but the Minister of Railways yesterday submitted a new statement. I shall not deal with the whole of the liabilities set out in that statement but only with the annual charges. If my hon. friend will look at his own statement to be found on page 1443 of Hansard I will ask him this question: What does he propose to do with the lake Superior branch bonds to the amount of $301,320 annual interest?

The branch was made part of the Government's system long ago, so this transaction has nothing to do with that.

speechtext:
One parting shot and
I am done with this branch of the subject. We have been told by the Government that we have no alternative than to take over the Grand Trunk railway. In the light of the figures which have been furnished to us and all the explanations which have been given I take issue with my hon. friends and I say there is an alternative. I do not think the Government should have gone to the Grand Trunk, as it has been shown here they have done, and said: " Come here, we want you." The Government should have introduced a little business sense into this transaction and the alternative they could have employed was to use ordinary business principles. Here we are with the proprietors in England owning a railway in Canada-some of them preferred shareholders, others ordinary share-

holders, and others bondholders, hut all having security.
Instead of offering such an agreement as this the Government should first have found out whether the Grand Trunk is obligated to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I believe it is a point of law whether the Government has broken its contract with the Grand Trunk in that regard. Now, if the Grand Trunk is obligated to the Grand Trunk Pacific, it is evident that the Grand Trunk cannot pay and that if something was not done it would go into the hands of a receiver. I frankly admit that to allow the Grand Trunk to go into the hands of a receiver would lead us nowhere. The alternative is this: the Government should have required the 'bondholders of the Grand Trunk to forego their interest for 2 years and allow to continue, say, fifteen or twenty years. This would have resulted in the releasing of a large amount of cash, and then we could have handed back the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Government owning the minority stock. The Grand Trunk people should then have been told: "You have to help us in this thing ", Hon. members opposite have tried to cast an odium upon members on this side; they have endeavoured to substantiate the argument that we are opposed to public ownership. That is simply a blind to deceive the people. My sympathies are not with the bondholders in England; they are with the Canadian taxpayers. That is my sugges-tioh, then, as to what should have been done; no sound business man would say otherwise. The way that we are proposing to treat these 'bondholders in England smells of Max Aitken's pudding; it is simply an abomination.

speechtext:
Wpll, it is really unfortunate that the hon. member is not Minister of Finance; he could borrow money for nothing. I had my hopes raised-I must say, unnecessarily raised-when the hon. member got up and announced that he had an alternative policy to suggest. For weeks I have been waiting hopefully and anxiously for some such suggestion, and knowing the hon. member to be a courteous gentleman I was quite sure that we were in for something at last that would give us food for thought.
Now, his alternative policy is this: He says first that we should have found out whether the Grand Trunk was bound to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Well, I am glad to be able to inform the hon.
4 p.m. member that we did find that out and that we found that they were bound. In fact, we never had any doubt about that since away back in 1903; so on that point the hon. gentleman's soul may rest at ease.
Then, he says, we should also ascertain whether or not the Government had broken its contract with the Grand Trunk. We .-found that out also. We found that the Government had broken no contract; that it had fulfilled, and more that fulfilled, all its contracts, but notwithstanding the utmost goodwill and co-operation on the part of the Government the enterprise so unfortunately launched by hon. gentlemen opposite fifteen years ago cannot be saved. So as far as that goes the hon. member and I are on the same ground: All that he asks that we find out was attended to in due time; there rests no doubt whatsoever on the subject.
He says also that the debenture holders -the bondholders, as he describes them-* of the Grand Trunk should forego their interest for twenty years. Well, that would be very nice indeed for us. But what reason has the hon. gentleman to think that debenture holders who have drawn their interest every year since the debenture was issued-who drew it even during the last two years of war-would be ready to forego their interest when they know that they can run the system and pay the interest on the bonds? It would be a very happy thing for Canada if we could get people to give us money for nothing or pro-

perty for nothing; if that were the case we would not to-day be trying to float a Victory Loan at five and a half per cent. Of course, another way would be to ask the company to hand us over the road for nothing. That also would be very good, but it was not along lines like that that the hon. gentleman and his friends proceeded in 1903 or 1904, or, indeed, ever in history. In a word, the phantasma that the hon. gentleman has before him does not indicate that he knows the real essence of the solution of a complicated business problem. What has the Government before it in the way of investigation and report? What has it in the way of the opinion of expert men to warrant its saying to those who have the first mortgage on the whole Grand Trunk system: " Stand without your interest for' twenty years?" We anchor our policy to an expert report, which hon. gentlemen have been lauding and commending for the last two or three years, including, I think, the hon. member himself (Mr. Fournier). This report says that the debenture holders are entitled to and can collect their interest. It says also that all those above, the holders of the proprietary rights of the company, are entitled to an annual payment from this company of a substantial payment of $3,600,000- which sum they have drawn on an average for ten years-and to an increase of that substantial proportion within a few years by forty or fifty per cent. We base our policy upon that; we do not base it upon any mere miasma; upon any suggestion that people are going to make presents to this country that they do not have to make. We are not actuated by sympathy for the Grand Trunk shareholders or for any one else; we are actuated by principles of decency and justice. We do not feel that we should arbitrarily decide that property owned by other people is worthless. We had a lecture on that subject from my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) last night; he said that such a course would be arbitrary and ruthless, or words to that effect. We feel that when we acquire property which we believe it to be in the interests of the country to acquire under the present unfortunate conditions, we ought to submit to judicial determination, if we are not able to agree upon it, the question of what that property is worth.

speechtext:
The Minister of Railways the other night referred to a subject which is worthy of careful thought and consideration-the question of taxation and municipal assessment as affecting this system.

All of the property is assessable in the different cities, towns and villages in Canada through which the road passes, and I. should like to know what value for assessment purposes the different assessors have put upon the Grand Trunk itself apart from the Grand Trunk Pacific or the subsidiary companies in the United States and what taxes the Grand Trunk paid last year in the different cities, towns and villages. Clause 3 gives us perhaps wider scope for dealing with the different phases of the transaction than any other clause of the Bill. The minister says that he is going to hold this property in a certain receptacle which he is going to call the Grand Trunk Railway Company, 'but he says that everything in that receptacle belongs to the Government to all intents and purposes, and he resents the idea that any one should say that it is not absolute government ownership. Although the minister claims that this property belongs to the Government, nevertheless we are going to ignore section 125 of the British North America Act, and we are going to pay taxes on everything in that receptacle belonging to the company. If that is part of the bargain, that is something that the people of Canada who have to pay the taxes ought to know. They ought to know how much taxes they have-to pay. They should not pay any, but the minister 'says that he is going to make a present to all the municipalities through whose lands these roads run. He does not pay the taxes; the Canadian people pay them. We want to know what is the size of the present that he is going to have the people of Canada make to the wealthy city of Montreal, the equally wealthy cities of Toronto and Kingston, and all the other wealthy towns. How much have my poor fishermen in Nova Sootia to contribute to the city of Toronto? How much are the people of Canada going to pay illegally? I say "illegally," because section 125 says that if we own a property as government property, we pay no taxes on it. But the minister broke in the other night to allay a false report as he called it that was going abroad, and he said that the country was to pay taxes on this undertaking. We want to know the extent of his liberality to people who live along the track of the Grand Trunk.

I think the question
of the hon. member is absurd. He states that the Government intend making a present to these municipalities. The hon. member knows that tifcm Grand Trunk railway system is in exactly the same position as the Canadian

Pacific or the Canadian Northern; it has always paid taxes. Does he mean now to say that we should take away from the municipalities a right that they have had in accordance with the laws of this country that -a private corporation should be taxed. This is a private company, the stock of which we are purchasing, so that we are the owners through the stock system. The hon. member thinks it a terrible affair that we are not going now to deprive these municipalities of the taxes the company has been paying and to put this company in a different position from that in which the Canadian Pacific has been in the past. The taxes paid by the Grand Trunk are given in the 'statistics contained in the blue-book on railway statistics and amount to $799,377.90. The hon. member thinks it a crime now that we should not act under the British North America Act and deprive these municipalities in the several provinces of these taxes. The Government should carry out the policy of paying the taxes just as the company has done in the past and as it is entitled to do under the law. The company pays taxes just the same as before. The Canadian Northern Railway Company last year paid taxes, as appears on page 73 of the Railway Statistics, amounting to $434,488.02. The hon. member asked as to the assessed value of the Grand Trunk system. I have not that here. 1 suppose we could get that, but what difference does it make in this transaction? This is not a question of the assessed value.

speechtext: Do you mean to say they were responsible for all this?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Liberal Government were responsible for every dollar of it. They forced the thing through, and we are in the position we are in to-day in consequence. We are trying to save the wreck that they made of the whole railway situ-
ation. We are trying to link up with the Grand Trunk in order that we may have a complete system and stop the losses that are occurring on account of having a jug-handled system through the policy of the leader of the Government and the Minister of Finance of that day. That is the situation. How can we make this road pay if we have not connections in the East, in Ontario and Quebec? Without those connections it is impossible for us to continue. The Grand Trunk system which we are taking over has been able in the past to pay dividends, and is now, and I believe in the future will be able not only to pay the dividends which it has paid in the past, but that the interchange of traffic between what is now the Grand Trunk system and the Canadian National system will not only help the Grand Trunk very materially and the National system, but will decrease the cost of management. Surely the only remedy for the railway situation in which we find ourselves to-day is to take over this road in order, at all events, to make ends meet instead of having to ask Parliament every year to make good an operating loss of $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific and of at least $6,000,000 on the Transcontinental. For the life of me I cannot see any reason why this proposed legislation should not go through, unless the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite is, as I believe it is, and as was advocated by my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), to let the road go into the hands of a receiver. He knows just as well as I do that that means the road will go to the Canadian Pacific Railway. If we refuse this offer now, the Grand Trunk can or will make an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway, who will take the Grand Trunk over. I have heard this argument made by hon. gentlemen opposite, by the leader of the Opposition, for one, I believe: The Canadian Pacific will have to come to this Parliament for legislation before they can take over the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition, the real leader of the Opposition, says, Hear, hear. He says the Canadian Pacific could not take over the Grand Trunk without first coming to this Parliament for legislation. Let me tell him that the Canadian Pacific has taken over railway corporations in the past and steamship companies. Public opinion at the time would not stand for it, but the Canadian Pacific managed to get other parties to secure the stock indirectly. Some holding or trust company would secure the stock, and ap-
/

parently to the outside world the Canadian Pacific would be fighting this holding company which it really controlled. After a while it would leak out that the Canadian Pacific owned and controlled the other company. They'have got it, and that is the end of it. The policy of the leader of the Opposition, or of the two leaders of the Opposition at the present time is this: First, wait for time. Now waiting for time means handing over the Grand Trunk to the Canadian Pacific. Secondly, they say: If you cannot do that, let the road go into the hands of a receiver. That also means going into the hands of the Canadian Pacific. I think it would be better if the hon. gentlemen would come out in the open and say: We want these roads to go under the control and operation of the Canadian Pacific.
So far as I am concerned, my position is this: We cannot continue to operate these roads at such a. loss. The people of this country would not stand for it. We can only continue to operate the roads we have by taking over the Grand Trunk. By consolidating the roads I am confident we can operate them successfully and in the interests of the public.

speechtext: If we appoint a competent Board of Management comprising men of the highest ability we can operate them at present rates and make just as much money as the Canadian Pacific Railway. Under such a management I have no doubt whatever that the system could be made a success. There can be no difference in the management of the railways as between a private corporation and the Government if men of the same standard of ability and business acumen are appointed in either case.

It is hardly fair to expect me to answer that question offhand. What I do say is that we shall combine in one system the Canadian Northern Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway, three large systems, and that there should be appointed at least half a dozen of the very best railway men to operate the combination. Personally, I am sure that from the three systems we should foe able to select those men. In any event, their appointment will be decided when the proper time arrives. I do know that on the Intercolonial railway we had a number of excellent men who undoubtedly would be able, from their great experience, to operate a railway system successfully, and I have also come in contact with some of the ablest men in connection with the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk railway. However, if by any possibility we cannot obtain suitable men from these systems the Government is in a position to secure them no matter from what source they may come. Hon. gentlemen opposite are apprehensive; they think the Government cannot make a success of the system. Well, that is merely a reflection on the members themselves; for, unless there is interference on the part of members of Parliament, there should be absolutely no difference between the management under a private corporation and under the Government if equally competent men are appointed to administer the affairs of the system.
Mr. iBURNHAM: Is it not true that in a magnificent speech the minister established the fact that Parliament, by various means, made an appalling mess of the whole situation from the beginning?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
What I have said in
this House is that the appalling mess in connection with the railways was a legacy inherited by this Government from the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and we are struggling to the utmost of our ability to make the best of the situation. By consolidating the railroads we shall relieve the country from the large annual loss which it has had to bear as a result of the disjointed condition of the Canadian railways. My candid opinion is that by a vigilant oversight of the operations of the system, and under the economical management of competent men who know their business,

freight rates will he kept down, and in future, as the population increases, the people will enjoy cheaper rates instead of suffering, while millions of dollars are made by a private corporation. If we get control of the railway and have a consolidated system there is no doubt that we shall be able to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway, not injuring that concern, for that would be the last thing I should want to do. They can work harmoniously with our system in the interests of both railways and also .of the people at large.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Certainly; this is a union and therefore an economy.
- Mr. McKENZIE: There is no necessity for this union. Hon. gentlemen speak as if they had no roads in Ontario. They have two main lines running right through this great province; they have the Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental railway. Will it be said that it is necessary to make a success of Government ownership in Ontario to. have three parallel lines with their branches? That is the position that exists here to-day. If the hon. gentleman says it is necessary I never heard any such argument before. There is nobody saying to-day but that the Intercolonial is quite capable of looking after the traffic along that line. There is no need-there cannot be-of adding this particular line to the Intercolonial because the Minister of Railways says that every part of this system is to be used in a business manner. When he is asked if freights are to be routed to St. John or Halifax, he says that will be entirely for the management; the management will have to do all that; I have nothing to do with it. But a few days later he finds that there is an election in Carleton, N.B., that he has a candidate in the field, that he is sending three ministers down there to speak for that candidate. He makes a speech in this House and he says: " I will see to i% that traffic is routed to the Maritime Provinces. I would like to see the agent who would go out for Grand Trunk freight and divert it to Portland, if I am alive. I will see to it that he is dismissed, not next day, but that night; I will not wait until next day." The Minister of Railways in one breath is going to put the whole business into the hands of the most competent railway man he can find in America, and in the next breath he says that he must do it himself, that if freight is diverted in the slightest degree he will dismiss the officer of the road who allows it.
The intention of the Minister of Railways is to get one huge railway monopoly under his control entirely for political purposes. But my simple, innocent question was this: "Are we going to be paying taxes on this road after it becomes a Government railway?" He breaks forth in fury over the heterodoxy when I suggest that Government property should stop paying taxes. Does the Intercolonial pay any taxes? He
must answer that it does not pay one cent of taxes anywhere from Sydney to Montreal. Wherein does it differ then from any other road that is owned by the Government? The people are going to reason this thing out. The minister will not tolerate for one moment to have it said that the method or practice by which he is getting hold of these roads does not give him Government ownership. This road is either owned by the Government or it is not. If it is owned by the Government it should not pay taxes. If it does not belong to the Government of course it will have to pay taxes. There are parts of the Intercolonial railway that at one time did not belong to the Intercolonial. There was at one time a road called the Eastern Extension owned by a private company running from New Glasgow to the strait of Canso. It was subject to local laws and paid taxes. But somewhere around 1882, 1883, or perhaps as late as 1885, it became the property of the Government and a part of the Intercolonial. Did that section of the road pay any taxes after that? Not one dollar. It was made a part of the Intercolonial and it became free from taxation. That is a case in point exactly. If the Eastern Extension Railway Company ceased to pay taxes when it became the property of the Government, what is the logic by which the Grand Trunk, when it becomes the property of the Government, is to continue to pay taxes? There is no sense in it, there is no law for it and it is absolutely in violation of the constitution if it is done. One would think that I was making this law. It is section 125 of the British North America Act which enacts that any Government property either in a province or the Dominion, shall not pay taxes.	-
This getting hold of the stock of the Grand Trunk or Canadian Northern is simply a means to an, end. We are not buying that stock because we want to have it. We do not want it. It is no good, it does not pay any dividend, it is not an inviting speculation for the Government and they would not buy a dollar's worth of it for the sake of owning the stock. It is a way they take of owning the railway.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Very good. Then last year they owned the railway, the rolling stock, and everything about it, and they took possession of it. Therefore, if,we are to believe their argument, is it not, to all intents and purposes, exactly in the same box as the Intercolonial railway? There



is not a shadow of a difference between them except, as I said before, we are going to hold the Grand Trunk in this receptacle called the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and we are going to hold the Canadian Northern in the receptacle called the Canadian Northern Railway Company; we own everything that is in both those receptacles, according to hon. gentlemen opposite. Therefore, the law that applies to govern-mentowned companies or government-owned property applies here and we should not pay any taxes at all. Now hon. gentlemen try to make a great deal of fuss about conditions on the Intercolonial railway. Those who know the history of this country are aware that Nova Scotia, at all events, was not anxious to come into Confederation and never wanted to do so. People would think that we Nova Scotians shoved ourselves upon Confederation and that we came begging, upon favourable conditions with respect to the Intercolonial railway. Not at all; we were coaxed into Confederation. The Intercolonial was offered as an inducement to come in and we were assured that we would always have certain rights and conditions in regard to that road that would compensate us for what we were losing. Hon. gentlemen know that before Confederation the Maritime Provinces dealt largely with the United States. We sent our coal there free of duty; we sent our fish there free of duty; we had a magnificent trade with the United States. All of that was cut off when we entered Confederation with a tariff wall and we were joined to Quebec and Ontario. In respect to the goods that we sent and received by water we were told that we would have the same convenience back and forth on the Intercolonial. That was the condition under which we came into Confederation and under which that road was built. Now, if the Government of Canada is living up to a certain extent to the terms of Confederation and the terms with regard to the Intercolonial, why should I be told by the President of the Privy Council, when I speak about paying or not paying local rates upon this railway, "Oh, when you beggars in the Maritime Provinces pay your freight rates properly then it will be time enough for you to talk about what is being done on the Intercolonial." That is not common sense from a member of the Government. We are under no obligation and we are looking for no favours in this matter- we are looking for constitutional rights and constitutional privileges. I say to the Government that when millions upon millions of dollars worth of [Mr. McKenzie.!
property are owned by the people of the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the Canadian Constitution says that that property shall not pay any taxes, the Government has no business to make the people in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec pay taxes on other property outside of their own when on like kind of property in their own provinces they pay no taxes at all on government owned property. That is why I asked the minister the question " What taxes shall we have to pay on the Grand Trunk and upon the Canadian Northern?" Hundreds of thousands of dollars, possibly millions of dollars, are to he paid altogether-I do not know how much the Canadian people will have to pay out of their own pocket, out of the earnings of these roads- when the constitution of the country says they shall not pay one cent. What is the Minister of Railways blowing and blustering about as to the cost to the country to build one particular road or another? That is not an answer to my question. I want to know clearly and distinctly how he proposes to get out of the provision of the Constitution which provides we shall not pay any taxes upon government owned property? He says that we shall go on paying those taxes as is now done. If he says we are going to pay the taxes, then he must admit that we do not own the property, because it is a right or a prerogative, of the Crown, if you please, that it shall not be taxed-anyway, the Crown shall not tax itself. There is where the principle came in that government property is exempt from taxation. Wise, or unwise, it is the law, and nobody ever found any fault with it. If that provision is in the Act and if it applies to the Intercolonial railway, I see no good logic, reason or law, why the same principle should not apply to every mile-of railway that the Government of Canada will own in this country.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It seems to me, if I might make the observation, that we are losing sight of the fact that those who take the most vital interest in the provision under discussion are the people of this country. The Canadian people have got to pay the taxes; they are the ones who must bear the burden; and for my part, as a patriotic Canadian and as a man who never expects to get back to this House-
Some hon. MEMBERS; Oh, oh.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: -I nevertheless unhesitatingly say that although it may mean suicide to myself, we ought to go to the country and let the people speak on this question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Last night 1 drew the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the extraordinary wording of this section and the unlimited powers which it gives the Government. I should like to read the section and ask if the minister has drafted the amendment which I understood he was to prepare and submit to the House to-day. The section reads:
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests, comprised in the Grand Trunk System, and, including the terms and provisions hereinafter set forth, may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon.
In reading that section one would notice that the reference to " terms and provisions
92i	*
hereinafter set forth " is in the nature of a parenthetical clause, and if the sentence were read with that clause transposed it would run as follows:
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests, comprised in the Grand Trunk System, and may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon, including the term's and provisions hereinafter set forth.
I think the minister will agree that he is asking Parliament to give the Government far too much latitude in connection with the agreement. Before I propose any change in the clause by the striking out of some of its words, I should be glad to hear whether the minister has an amendment to offer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I stated yesterday that
I thought it might be well to amend the clause by providing that the terms and conditions of the agreement should be consistent with the terms and conditions set forth in the Bill. The intention is that the agreement shall be only so much more complete in detail as is necessary to carry out the strict intent of Parliament, and anything making that effect clearer I should be very glad to accept. I have not prepared an amendment, but I suggest that these words be added:
Such other terms and conditions not to be inconsistent with the provisions of this Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
In refusing the request of the leader of the Opposition that the agreement be placed on the Table, the Minister of the Interior is taking a course directly opposite to that which was taken by his leader (Sir Robert Borden) in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific legislation. On March 14, 1904-I quote from Hansard of that year, volume 1, page 7- Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, moved:
That the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both Houses of Parliament of the Dominion- of Canada, be taken into consideration on Monday next.
Mr. R. L. Borden, of Halifax, the leader of the Opposition, then said:
Before the motion is adopted I would like to bring to the attention of the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) the fact that reference is made in the speech to an agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, or gentlemen representing that company; and I would like to know if it is the intention of the Government to place that agreement upon the table of the House before the address is taken into consideration? As this is a subject of considerable importance, I should think it only right that tne House should have the advantage of perusing the agreement before we enter into consideration of the speech from the Throne.

My hon. friend will notice that the leader of the Opposition of that day proposed to hold up the Address until the Government had brought down that agreement in detail and laid it on the Table, so that the representatives of the people might see it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier replied as follows to the remarks of the leader of the Opposition :
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I may inform my hon.
friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the message he refers to will be laid on the Tab'e before the end of this sitting.
That is all we are asking to-day; that the agreement be .placed before the representatives of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I have not had time to look over that debate, but I am indebted to my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) for bringing the incident up; for it clearly sets out the principle that governed Parliament then and that governs Parliament now. The speech from the Throne was brought down and in it there was a statement that Parliament would be asked to ratify an agreement already entered into by the Government. The leader of the Opposition (Sir Robert Borden) of that day said: "Before we are asked to ratify an agreement which has -been entered into, we had better see it, because there is nothing in the speech from the Throne which indicates what the agreement contains." In that case, had the agreement not been brought down, there would have been nothing before Parliament on which to base a discussion-not even the principles of the agreement, to say nothing of its precise terms. It was only common sense that an agreement entered into should be laid before the House if it was to be discussed, because, I repeat, the speech from the Throne embodied nothing at all that could be the basis of a discussion in Parliament. But here we 'have everything. Here we have what the agreement is to contain, all that is felt to foe essential; and there is another great difference as well: Parliament has the privilege of adding anything that it may desire. Everything is before Parliament; the door is open. In that case the dqor was closed; the agreement had been signed. The difference between the two cases is really so great that they are hardly comparable.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend forgets that authority had been given at the previous session of Parliament for the making of a certain agreement. The Grand Trunk people subsequently came before the Government and asked for a change in that agreement and Parliament was called to give the Government authority to ratify the change.

Mr. iMEIGHEN:	Very good; was it not
well that Parliament should know what the proposed change was? The speech from the Throne did not say to Parliament what it was. But we say to Parliament, in this Bill,/what the agreement is to be; this (Bill contains the agreement. It does not contain the necessary details that must be embodied in an agreement, but it contains the essential principles thereof and may contain any detail that Parliament wants it to contain. But in the case the hon. gentleman mentions, Parliament had nothing at all before it to discuss-merely the fact that there was a change in agreement to be brought down. Parliament had been asked to authorize the Government to enter into an agreement and Parliament agreed to do so; is not that just the same as her%J Parliament had given the authority, just as Parliament is being asked to give the authority now.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, and the Government
of the day refused to change that agreement until they came before the representatives of the people for authority to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly, and when we enter into an agreement under exactly the same conditions, having been authorized by Parliament to do it, not only must we refuse to change or amend it without the authority of Parliament; vve absolutely could not do so; we would be legally powerless to change it. So with the Government of that day; any change would 5 p.m. have been wholly ineffectual until Parliament had approved. It is just the same in this case; we can make only that agreement which we are authorized to make, just as the Government of that day could make only the agreement that it was authorized to make. Subsequently the agreement was changed, but, as I have said, the alteration was wholly ineffectual until it had been ratified by Parliament.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
May I direct the minister's attention to what seems to be an exact parallel? The Treaty of Peace was an agreement drawn and signed by the parties to it. It was thought necessary, after that agreement had been signed, to summon this session of Parliament for the .express purpose of ratifying it. There were two distinct acts: First, the act of drawing the agreement and having it signed; second, the calling of Parliament together for the purpose of giving its approval to the agreement. Now, all that gentlemen on this side are asking is that what the Government found it necessary to do in connection, with

a treaty relating to questions outside of .Canada, they do in regard to this question particularly affecting our own country-one of the most important questions that this Parliament has ever had to consider.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
parallel is rather destructive of his argument. Was there any prior authority on the part of Parliament to enter into the Treaty of Peace? Had there been, what would have been the need of ratification? If Parliament, before the Treaty of Peace was made, could have laid down the lines and the essential provisions of the treaty, that would have been a far greater privilege on the part of Parliament than that of subsequent ratification, when alteration would be difficult if not impossible. Here the facilities for alteration are right before us. Have I made it clear? Had Parliament been able to authorize in advance the provisions of that treaty, Parliament would have had a free hand and would have been in a much stronger position than it was in with the mere right of ratification. In this case, there shall be no need of ratification afterwards because we authorize before.
In the case brought up by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Eobb) where Parliament was asked to authorize making an agreement along certain lines, the Government made the agreement along those lines. Was that a flouting of the people's rights as the hon. gentleman lectured us? Were the people's rights flouted at that time? Having made the agreement along the lines authorized by Parliament, did the Government of that day come before Parliament and ask for ratification of that agreement? They came to Parliament only when they sought authorization; they never came back for ratification of an agreement that they bad been authorized to make.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I think I read to the hon. gentleman the clause containing the agreement in relation to the National Transcontinental railway. That clause expressly provided that that agreement came into effect only when it was ratified by this Parliament. I suggested a clause in identical terms to be inserted in this particular Bill and an agreement made under it. The minister refused to accept it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The agreement provided that it came into effect only when ratified by Parliament; it could not provide otherwise. So far as the agreement was made in advance, it could come into effect only when ratified by Parliament.
That was done in one case to which the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon referred in which the agreement was made in advance. There are two ways of doing this, and both have been practised many times, but we must be governed by circumstances. One method is just as good, just as equitable and just as frequently, if not more frequently used than the other. Indeed, the almost universal practice is for Parliament to lay down the main lines and principles, and then the details following out those principles exactly are worked out by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I should like to draw the minister's attention to the other point of which I spoke last night, namely, that after the agreement had been drawn up by the Government and the Grand Trunk, the Government still reserves to the shareholders of that company the right to ratify that agreement, but the Government denies a similar right to the representatives of the people in this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Because we lay down
the lines of the agreement. Surely that is a stronger position than being asked to ratify it after it is made. We lay down the lines; the shareholders have not been consulted at all. We lay down the lines of the agreement, everything essential in it and everything we want.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is a difference between laying down lines and general principles and laying down specific terms.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Let the (hon. member bring forward any terms he wants to suggest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Everything that is laid down in a general way by this Parliament, everything that is done under this Bill if it becomes law, will be known to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Eailway Company before they are asked to give their consent to that agreement. We on this side contend that if the Government is going to reserve to the Grand Trunk shareholders a right, it should of necessity reserve, the same right to the people of Canada. What becomes of Parliament, of responsible government, of any of the provisions which have been made in the constitution for safeguarding the Tights of the people, if private shareholders and corporations are to be given privileges that the people's own representatives in Parliament are denied?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The very striking
difference between the two positions, that

is, between what took place in 1903 and what is taking place now is this, and to my mind it is very important. We are having put through this House now what is called an enabling Bill giving to the Government certain powers to do certain things, for instance, to make an agreement -with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, 'but the terms of the agreement and the agreement itself are not before us at all. We are, therefore, saying to the Government simply: Go and make an agreement, whatever agreement you think proper to make. It is true there are certain general principles laid down in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Very definite principles.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But we give the Government a free hand to make an agreement, which will come into effect just as soon as the shareholders are willing to accept the conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No free hand about it.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I move to amend clause 3 of the Bill by inserting after the word "conditions" in the fifth line of the said clause, the following words: "not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act."

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That amendment does not mean anything; it means simply that no agreement could be drawn up that would be inconsistent with the provisions of this Bill, or that if any agreement were drawn up inconsistent with the provisions of the Bill, it would not be a legal agreement. It is a huge farce of an amendment. There is no other way of qualifying it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) said last night that this would be a considerable improvement.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If my hon. friend feels happy over anything he may get from the leader of the Opposition, I certainly do not begrudge him his few moments of happiness.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I believe the leader of the Opposition is right on that point, and I am glad to have the opportunity of commending his suggestion.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
A very happy disposition must he coming over my hon. friend for him to say the leader of the Opposition is right. Surely that must be classed as another improvement. The contention that is made on this side with regard to clause 3, if I have followed the discussion aright, is that the Government should not have the power to put in the agreement other terms

and conditions which may not be known to the people of Canada, and secondly, that the people of Canada have the same right as the shareholders of the Grand Trunk. The minister says: " It is all right. It has been done in the past.' Many things have been done in the pasit that must not be repeated in the present, and certainly will not be repeated in the future.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend agrees
with me. Let me put it this way: The Government is .acting as solicitor or counsel for the people, charged by the people to draw up the agreement with the Grand Trunk. Another counsel is empowered by the Grand Trunk shareholders to draw up the agreement for them. The Government say to the people, their clients, "We will draw up the agreement according to the powers that you give us, but as your counsel will have the right to put in the agreement other terms and conditions as we may deem wise." The people say to the Government: " But we want to read over that agreement before we attach our signature to it." Counsel, the Government, replies: " No. You are empowering us to sign your name and you will not have the right to read over the agreement. Then the people say, " The shareholders of the Grand Trunk, the other parties to this agreement, will have the right of reading it over before their signatures are affixed to it. Why should we not have that power?" The Government answers, " Because we may require to put in other terms and conditions which we cannot tell you of at present, but which will not !be inconsistent with the power you give us to sign your name."
I put it to the Government, is it fair to put their clients, the people of Canada, in that position? Should not the people of Canada be on exactly the same footing as the shareholders of the Grand Trunk, the other parties to the agreement, and have the right to lead it over before their signature is attached? I may be wrong, but I take it that that is what was in the mind of the leader of the Opposition when speaking. I can very readily understand, him saying that the words suggested " Not inconsistent with the provisions- of this Act " are an improvement, because the Government -before did not even want to give the people of Canada the right to say that nothing should be put in the agreement except what was consistent with the provisions of this Act, Now the Government say to the people: " Wc will not put in the agreement any terms and
conditions which are not consistent with the powers which you give us, but we will put in other terms and conditions than those perhaps with which you are familiar. We take it that the power you have given us to sign your name empowers us to put -in other terms and conditions in the agreement, which you shall not see or know of before you become bound thereby." I think the position which the Government is asking the people of Canada to assume is an unjust position. It is a position that no private individual would be asked to assume, and we should apply the same rule to a body of individuals that we apply to an individual. The body of individuals -in this case is the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
First, with regard to the amendment. It might conceivably be argued, and I have no doubt that this is what was in the mind of the leader of the Opposition last evening, that as the clause reads at present the power of putting in other terms and conditions, being cumulative, did not forbid terms and conditions even differing from the terms and conditions here. As that might conceivably be argued, possibly not effectually argued, it is certainly an improvement to put those words in. Now the hon. gentleman says that we should have done as was done in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific in the 1903 case, the only -case, as I am informed, but not as was done in the second case-I am looking into that to be sure I am right. He says we should have done what was done in 1903, have had the agreement made, and then brought it down to Parliament for ratification. That is one method; this is another method. Let us examine which is the best from the standpoint of Parliament, and this is very important. When you come down to Parliament with an agreement signed and sealed for ratification what is the function of Parliament? It is to take that agreement as it is or to let that agreement go. Parliament's hands are virtually tied, because the Government of the day is committed. It has signed and sealed all the terms and details and Parliament has no say at all. It is a case of Parliament taking it or leaving it. That was one of the main criticisms levelled at the -plan of the Government in 1903. We have no desire to emulate the course pursued in 1903 any further than is constitutionally necessary. In this case we have followed the other plan, which has been frequently adopted. Parliament has everything before it; there is nothing in the world kept from Parliament-. Parliament can in-

sort, can add, or subtract. The whole field is before Parliament. We lay down here certain provisions. It is for Parliament to add to them or strike them out. Is that not a far better position to put Parliament in than to come here with a hard-and-fast agreement, with everything cut-and-dried, and say to Parliament: "There is the agreement. We have made it and it is for you to turn us out or leave us in. Take the agreement just as it is, or leave it just as it is." I submit that much the better position to put Parliament in the position Parliament is in to-day, where Parliament has a free hand to insert more clauses than are here or to take from clauses which are provided to be enacted in the agreement.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman claim that Parliament is absolutely free now to deal with this agreement in any way it pleases other than by dismissing the Government? The hon. gentleman has stated that all the material parts of the agreement are set forth in tihe correspondence, which amounts to an agreement with the Grand Trunk *Company. Does he claim that he can put aside all that correspondence and that we can do anything we like, with the freedom which he suggests? We can only do it by dismissing the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Probably, if the Government could not accept the suggestion of Parliament, it might have to go. But the Government can accept the suggestions of Parliament.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not if they are at variance with what the hon. gentleman has already contracted for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
We have entered into nothing binding with the Grand Trunk Company in any sense whatever. There is nothing in the nature of a final agreement such as the hon. member entered into in 1903. Parliament may now make suggestions which may he quite acceptable to the Government. It may make suggestions which might prove quite acceptable to both the Grand Trunk and the Government; or, on the other hand, suggestions which might be acceptable to us and not to the Grand Trunk, and we are at liberty to assert that the Grand Trunk would not be bound to accept them. Parliament is free. It is infinitely freer to-day than it was in 1903. Parliament has the case presented to it in a form which I think it will appreciate,. and is in a much better position than it occupied in 1903, when all it could do was

to accept the Government's proposition as it was, or let the thing go altogether.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has entirely changed his ground. Throughout the debate he has been telling us that all the essentials of the agreement with the Grand Trunk are before us, and that the Government have come to an understanding with them. Now he practically tells us that there is no understanding with the Grand Trunk and that we are free to do as we like. That is	an	absolute change	of ground.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is no obduracy on either side. Possibly something can be suggested in the public interest which would be acceptable to them, hut no door is shut against them. If Parliament sees fit to make any suggestions it is perfectly at liberty to do so. Is not that a good position for Parliament to be in? We could not come before Parliament any sooner, and we are very glad that we did not come later. We did not go to the extent to which my hon. friend did:, and get the thing into such a shape that the pruning knife could not be applied, everything being hard and fast, cut and dried, leaving Parliament with nothing but an option to accept the proposi-'tion or let it go altogether. There is no difficulty now in the way of Parliament's making any amendment it deems desirable. Any amendment offered may be acceptable to the Grand Trunk or it may not, and we may insist on it even if it is not acceptable to them. What freer position could Parliament be in? It is true the letter is signed, but that does not say that there cannot be any alteration if Parliament insists upon it, nor that there cannot be any modification, that may he acceptable to both sides. That is absolutely the right position for Parliament to be in.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister has repeatedly stated that we have the agreement before us in all its essentials, and now he says that there is no agreement and that we are free to do what we like. I must say that such an entire change .in the attitude of the hon. gentleman is astonishing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is no change.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister has divined correctly what was in my mind last night. 1 suggested that the language here was much too wide. The clause reads:
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests comprised in the Grand Trunk System, and. including the terms and provision hereinafter set forth, may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon.

I pointed out that that gave power to introduce into the agreement any terms irrespective of the provisions of this Bill. The minister has realized the force of that contention and has suggested a 'modification of the clause hy adding the words, "not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act." To that extent there is an improvement. But the hon. member (Mr. Devlin) has also caught what was in my mind and what I think is even more important than the suggestion which the minister has made, and that is, that these words, "may contain such other terms and conditions" together with the minister's addition, are altogether superfluous if the agreement is to he limited to the terms and conditions stated in the Act. The minister tells us that the Bill includes everything that will go into the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I did not say that; it includes the essentials.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Oh, well, there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: There is a contingency covered in the letter which is before Parliament, of October 9, which is not in the Bill but must necessarily go into the agreement. Suppose it is discovered after the arbitration award is made that there has been some undisclosed liability which has later turned1 up; provision must be made against such an event. That is the sort of detail that goes into the agreement, although it does not require to be set out in the Bill. If this committee thinks it worth while that a clause embodying even that detail should be put into the Bill there is no objection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I think it
would be desirable to embody just as much as is necessary. We have, two positions. The minister first tells us that the Bill contains all the terms and provisions that will go into the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The essential ones.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: He now qualifies it by adding the word, "essential." I should like to know what provisions other than the essential ones are necessary. What is the necessity of putting into the agreement provisions that are not essential?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
'There are provisions that go to carry out the evident intent of a Bill which Parliament passes, just as regulations are made by a department, approved by the Governor in Council, to carry out the intent of a Bill authorizing that department to do certain things. It is exactly
the same thing here. There is no difference either in principle or in method.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I think Parliament would be better secured in its rights if the minister would eliminate altogether the unnecessary words in this section: " May contain such other terms and conditions," together with his own suggestion, " not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If that were done the Government would be absolutely precluded from making any provision to safeguard the interests of the country. Take the Canadian Northern agreement which was authorized in the same way. I assure the hon. gentleman that if he goes through the terms of that agreement he will find every detail following out the general authorization of the Act. Every one of those details is inserted to safeguard the interest of the public. Would it have been wise to have forbidden that to be done? That is a matter that can be done after a most careful legal examination of the whole thing. The principles and terms, specific as you wish to make them, are here or can be put here. But it would be surely an act of folly to disarm the Governor in Council from making whatever safeguarding provisions may be necessary in the agreement.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior the other day, in answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) said that the agreement would not take effect until every shareholder of the Grand Trunk had surrendered his voting power.
