subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Every guaranteed stock shareholder.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Later on, in answer to a question by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier, he said that no provision had so far been made for granting a delay to the shareholders in surrendering that voting power.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No delay has been provided.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No delay has been provided and the hon. gentleman stated that the delay would be a subject to be taken care of in the agreement itself. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What page is that?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Hansard page 1132. I respectfully submit that the question <Jf the delay which will be granted to the shareholders to surrender their voting power is

an essential part of the agreement. If by the obstinacy of one shareholder the agree-*men can be destroyed or impeded, it is essential that this Parliament should put into the Bill specific delay which would he granted the shareholders. It was said to this House that the number of shareholders was very large-more than 100,000. The Government must enter into negotiations through the intermediary of the Grand .Trunk to get the surrender of their voting power. It may take a very long time, and the uncertainty as to the control taken by the Government will last very long. I would like to know if they have arrived at any decision upon this question of delay. How long do they wish to allow the shareholders to surrender their voting power? The question to which I refer is quoted at page 1132 of Hansard, second column. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) says:
What would be the situation if some of them refused to surrender their voting power?
Mr. Meighen:	Until that is done the agreement would not take effect.
Are we to be in the dark as to the time at which the agreement will take effect? Is it not essential for this committee to have a specific clause put into the Bill so that the people will know that at a certain day the bargain will be closed? If this clause is not put into the Bill, there is no bargain and we are without knowledge as to the time when the bargain will be completed. The Governor in Council may grant, one, two, three, four, five, or ten years to the shareholders to surrender their voting power. Without that the agreement will not have effect, according to the words of the Minister of Interior himself and I submit it is an essential part of the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am not surprised that the hon. gentleman asks the question because I do not think my statement in answer to the question of the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) was in the clearest possible form. The fact is this: The guaranteed shareholders must surrender their voting power but it would seem to me that the legal, effectual, execution of the agreement by the company would constitute this surrender of the voting power. In any event the Government take no risk whatsoever for the reason that in clause 4 there is the following proviso:
Provided that concurrently with such guarantee of dividends and interest upon the present guaranteed stock and the present debenture stocks, respectively, the voting powers at meetings of shareholders of the Grand Trunk .now

vested in or exercisable by the holders of the said stocks respectively shall cease and determine absolutely.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is confiscation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No, there can be no
confiscation because they must be parties to the arrangement by the effectual execution of the agreement on the part of the company. As soon as they have agreed that the agreement shall take effect their consent is obtained and immediately we give our guarantee and in pursuance of that agreement their voting power dies at once. They have authorized us to give that guarantee by themselves approving of the agreement. Is that clear to the hon. member?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I understand that the
agreement must be submitted for the approval of the shareholders and that by a vote of the majority-perhaps you may require two-thirds; I am not sure of that- clause 4 will be applied?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
There is in this clause a sort of confiscation of the vested rights of the shareholders who compose the minority and who may be against the surrendering of their voting power. Supposing there are 30,000 shareholders constituting a minority who do not want to surrender their voting power, does the minister say that by virtue of clause 4 which provides that their rights shall cease absolutely, there is not a sort of confiscation? The minority are against surrendering their rights. The minister says that by clause 4, in view of the position of the minority, their rights will cease absolutely when the majority shareholders have so decided. Is that right; is that just? I respectfully submit that it is not, and that the minister was more nearly right when he said the other day that we should induce the minority to surrender their voting power. He said that this inducement was to be offered in order that the transaction should not be impeded or absolutely destroyed by the obstinacy of some shareholders. Evidently he has changed his mind to-day.
IV'fr. MORPHY:	Is it not the universal
practice in every joint stock company or corporation for the by-laws to provide that in voting upon a question the majority shall rule?
If it were not. so and the minority were to receive special consideration it would be impossible to carry out an agreement with such a corporation, or company. Absolutely the only way, to my mind, that mergers, or unions-, or transfers of interests,

can possibly be brought about is by following that principle.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I have seen many cases in the courts where the shareholders constituting the minority have taken action to set aside the decision of the majority. The law that a majority shall rule is very well in the case of the administration of public affairs where you have voting at general elections, but when it comes to company law there are provisions which protect the rights of the shareholders constituting the minority.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Are there such provisions in this company, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The general law, the common law, is there.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Oh, no.
Mr. TRAHAN. You must protect the rights of every one. You cannot, by the common law, force a shareholder to sell his own property; and if by law you take the means of forcing a lot of shareholders to sell their property, that is a sort of confiscation. It is against this injustice that I protest and1 say that clause 4 is not just. I say that the question of the delay to be granted to the shareholders to surrender their voting powers should be determined in this Bill. Now, has the minister any idea of the delay which the Government intends to grant to the shareholders for the surrendering of their voting power?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's point is, first, we have no right to say to the minority shareholders, who may desire to refuse to surrender their voting power (the majority having agreed):	"We give
our guarantee and your voting power is gone." Well, I submit just what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Morphy) has said, which is the law, as I understand it, applicable to these shareholders and to all others: the shareholder of a company must allow that his rights are circumscribed by the statute governing his company and by the by-laws of that company. Is that not correct? So that if either the statute or the by-laws provide that the minority shareholders are hound by the will of the majority, or the minority to the extent of a third are bound by the will of a two-thirds majority, then if that two-thirds majority or bare majority, as the case may be, decide on a certain course, a minority shareholder has no right to complain, because that was the condition of his taking the stock; he is only
doing what he agreed he must do when he became a shareholder. He must submit to the by-laws and the statute governing the company, and if that provides that shareholders shall have a right by majority vote to do a certain thing that is the reason he must do that certain thing and he has no right to complain. The by-laws or the statute must so provide or the agreement cannot be effectually executed, and unless it is eSectually executed it amounts to nothing at all. Now, answering the hon. gentleman's second question, he appears to think that because we arbitrarily say:
" Your stock amounts to nothing, so far as voting power goes after we give our guarantee," we are asking them to agree to give up something for nothing. I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned that, and I am glad it occurred to his mind, because it affords me an opportunity to again refer to a point that was raised by way of complaint to the agreement by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), when the subject came up first. That hon. gentleman said1: " You have added some appreciation to the guaranteed stock by the impression of the Government's guarantee." That is correct, there is a measure of appreciation, but in return we are getting just what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Trahan) refers to; we are getting a surrender of the voting power.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: So in asking them to do that we are not asking to confiscate anything at all. We get a measure of appreciation, but nothing like what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) said it was, because 4 per cent guaranteed stock to-day oould not be argued to be worth more than about 69.

speechtext: How much?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

About 69. That stock with the Government's direct guarantee, may appreciate 2 to 3 per cent, or possibly more, but we are selling Government 5J per cent at 100. A 5J per cent at 100 is just the same as a 4 per cent at 72 and a fraction; if the hon. gentleman will figure it out. Now, the hon. gentleman knows that a Government direct bond is better in the market than a Government guaranteed bond by about 3 points, so there is no way of arguing it would be worth over 69. There is an appreciation; it could not be

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Before this
clause carries let us see just what it is proposed that we should enact. Getting rid of all superfluous words, -we find that this is the purport of the section:

Who is to determine whether these "other terms and conditions" are or are not inconsistent with the provisions- of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: In other words, the Governor in Council reserves that right to himself, but is unwilling to permit Parliament to expre-ss any opinion in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We are absolutely willing; we are inviting the hon. gentleman to give us a term and a condition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is the minister -prepared to say that before this agreement goes into force he will have it presented to Parliament, either at this or at a subsequent session, and allow Parliament to determine whether or not the conditions it contains are inconsistent with the provisions of this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister state it again so there may be no misunderstanding?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The minister has not answered the question that I put to him. I asked whether it was the intention to insert in this Bill a special clause specifying the length of the period within which the voting power could toe surrendered by the shareholders.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext: It is confiscated, then..

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I can. only say that we cannot bring the agreement down until it is complete, and I do not know when it will be complete. When it is, there will certainly be no delay in bringing it down.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The letter which the Minister of the Interior read to the House on the 10th of October is said to contain all the terms of the bargain. In reply to that letter the president of the road wrote the following under date of October 10:
I have taken communication of your letter of the 9th instant, relative to the proposed acquisition by the Government of Canada of the control of the Grand Trunk Railway system, which correctly embodies our understanding on the subject.
Everything that is in the bargain as agreed upon between these two gentlemen is found in the letter of the Minister of the Interior bearing date October 9, which is replied to by the letter which I have just read. All the terms of the bargain, then, were known to both parties on the 10th of October last; why is it now necessary to give to the Governor in Council power under this section to make other terms that [DOT] are not set forth in this correspondence? That is the effect of this section of the Bill. The last line and a quarter of the section is a distinct and separate sentence by ifc-self; you must import the word "agreement"-before the word "may," so that it will read:	,
The agreement may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon.
Now, why do we open the door to other conditions or terms of agreement than those mentioned in the letter read by the minister on October 10, and of which we know nothing? The minister should agree to strike out all the words after the word "forth" in the second last line; then we would have a clear and distinct enactment enabling us to carry out an agreement the terms of which are set forth in the letter to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals

I think the hon. member was present when the Minister of the Interior explained that it would be impossible to accept an amendment of that kind; that it would not be in the interest of the Government to do so, and one of the reasons given was this. In the agreement that may be made, the Government intend inserting a clause similar to that stated in the letter, as follows:
Should the Government, within three months after the making of the award, claim that there existed any liabilities of the Grand Trunk or of any* company comprised in the Grand Trunk system which were not disclosed to the Board of Arbitrators prior to the making of their award, the Government may within such period *of three months, apply to the Board of Arbitrators to amend their award, and the board may thereupon decide whether such liabilities existed and were disclosed to them, whether the amount of their award would or would not have been affected thereby, and the amount of the deduction, if any, to be made in respect thereof; and may amend their award accordingly.
In other words, without the words that are in that clause, the award would be final as soon as it was made. There is nothing in the clause that would allow the arbitrators to increase the award, but that clause was inserted in the letter as a protection to the Government. Some liabilities might turn up that were not disclosed before the arbitrators made their award and which, had the arbitrators known of them at the time, would have led to a lower award being given. If the Government are able within three months to show that there are further liabilities which would reduce the award, they have the right to go to the arbitrators and ask for a reduction of the award. If the amendment of the hon. member is accepted and these words are stricken out, the award would be final, and the country might suffer

a serious loss in consequence. The clause refers only to deductions in the award and not to increases.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I quite agree that there should be in the Bill a condition just exactly to the effect of the clause read from the letter, because it appears to he a concise condition that can be embodied in legislation. That condition is, that if anything is discovered within so many days after the filing of the award, that was omitted or overlooked, it is possible to go back for an amendment of the award. I see no reason why that should not be in the Hill if it is intended to be of any service at all, and ,1 would agree at once if it was necessary Jo have a clause added covering that ground. .Then we would know precisely what we are dealing with. What we are objecting to is *to have used in the Bill any loose language which may involve more than the committee iContemplates. My amendment is simply that the clause shall read thus:
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the company's properties and interests, comprised In the Grand Trunk system, and, including the terms and provisions hereinafter set forth.
I intend that the clause should' stop there. I have no objection to embodying the terms set forth in the letter as >a part of the arrangement because we have the letter and we know what it contains. But I object to saying to this Parliament and to the people of Canada that this agreement "may contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon." That does not seem sensible. What is the good of coming to us for terms, and then put in the Bill a provision that no matter what we may say in the Bill, the agreement "may' contain such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon"? That is not restricting the parties in any way, and they can do just as they please without coming to Parliament. That is why I am moving to strike out the words which give that wide latitude to the parties after they leave Parliament altogether.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I would; have hoped that my hon. friend would not find it necessary to move this amendment because it seems to me a direct challenge or dispute of the good faith of the Government. The only way we can carry on business is by a certain amount of trust amongst honourable men, and this clause appears to me fairly good drafting because it is giving power to plenipotentiaries so to speak, the executive, the Government, to carry out this agreement in accordance with the general

terms of the Bill. Any objections which my hon. friend now expresses seem to be got over by the amendment moved by the Minister of the Interior, that is to say, that the agreement shall not be inconsistent with the terms of the Act. In all agreements made by governments it is essential that an executive body-should be appointed to carry out the terms. Parliament is not sitting from day to day, Parliament adjourns for months at a time; and the whole thing might be held1 up by reason of the amendment which my hon. friend moved. That is to say, the plenipotentiaries, the ministers, would not be clothed with proper power, but rather with a scant language which might hamper them in carrying out the agreement. Everybody in this House knows that when a man gives a power of attorney to his friend or his banker, that power of attorney, in order to allow business to be carried out as it is intended and without restrictions and unnecessary limitations, goes very much further in its terms than is absolutely essential. In mining matters, for instance, and in all essentially big business affairs, a person who is given power of attorney will not act nowadays unless the power of attorney if in ample terms, although if it was carried out in bad faith some one might say the person giving the power of attorney would be almost selling his soul. But here we have a very important public agreement with power given to the Governor in Council to carry it out, and it is inconceivable to me that the Government should add anything that was not agreed to by Parliament if this Bill becomes law. To add to the Bill the terms proposed is a direct challenge of the good faith of the Government and I, for my part, hope that the amendment will not carry.

No, it is far more general. No terms were laid down there at all, the whole thing being left to the Governor in Council. There are other examples of that kind, but it is not worth while hunting them up, they are so numerous. In 1910 the whole terms that protected the Government were authorized to be left to the Governor in Council by Parliament. In the legislation before us only the details are left to the Governor in Council, so that wherever something has been left out or is not adequately covered or safeguarded it can be embodied in the agreement. There is nothing at all in that inconsistent with the terms of the Bill, which are the essential guiding principles of the agreement. If the hon. gentleman will look at chapter 7 of the statutes of 1903, which happens to be before me, he will find another example of the kind I have mentioned: " The kind of securities to be guaranteed as aforesaid," it says-this was providing for a guarantee of the Canadian Northern railway in that year by the Government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier-" and the forms thereof and the forms of the mortgage." Everything upon which the whole loan rests was left to the Governor in Council. What is the hon. gentleman smiling about? Does he mean to say that a mortgage security for millions of dollars is not an agreement of importance? It could scarcely be more so. The terms of it, the care with which it is drafted, the caution with which every possible defect is guarded against-nothing
could be of more consequence than these matters but they are all left to the Governor in Council without even a guiding principle. Yet the hon. gentleman stands aghast because after laying down guiding principles in this case we leave the details to be worked out by the Governor in Council.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Minister of the
Interior has told us repeatedly that the negotiations in connection with the taking over of the Grand Trunk have been in progress for the last two years or more, and that no member on this side of the House should be surprised at the terms because they have been well known for the last two years and there is nothing new about them. If it be true that for the last two years the Government have been negotiating for this purchase and that on the ninth day of this month they sat down after two years' deliberation and put the terms of agreement in a letter I think we on this side of the House have a right to suppose that the terms are really there. We are told by the minister who wrote the letter and who drafted the terms after two years' deliberation that the terms are there and that the president of the company, the other party to the agreement, writes on the 10th of October: " Yes, I have read your letter," and' it is implied that he has examined the terms, that he knows all about them, and that the letter of the minister does contain all the terms. Now, that Government which has carried on these negotiations and embodied the terms in a letter comes to this Parliament for authority to carry out those terms. We would expect them just to ask for power to carry through the agreement which they have reached and put in writing and to which they have subscribed their name. There could be no great objection to their asking for that power, but they are not satisfied with that. Not only do ' they ask for power to carry out that agreement, but they say: You will give us power not only to carry out this agreement, but also to make any other kind of agreement that we like that may be arrived at between the two parties. The Government are not satisfied to stand by the agreement signed on the 9th of October and submitted to this House on the following day. They say: We want full latitude to change our minds and make other agreements and other terms altogether, and we want power in reserve to make that agreement on the strength of the carte blanche that is given to us by this Parliament." Now, we are not satisfied with that. We say that in a big and critical transaction such as this, involving almost

incomprehensible money liabilities for the country, involving payments of money every year, the people of Canada, who pay the money, should know exactly what sort of an agreement they are entering into, and should know it through the voice of their representatives in Parliament.
That is why we on this side say that the power should be specific and that there should be no room for speculation. If the ministers have something further let them take time to consider it and come before Parliament when they have reached a definite understanding as to what powers they do require. Let them put it in the form of legislation and we will consider it. It is futile for us to spend our time deciding what the powers shall be and at the conclusion of our labours leave unlimited scope to the Government to do whatever they please. According to the argument of the minister and my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) we might as well say in half a dozen lines: The Government of Canada shall have power to purchase the Grand Trunk railway on such terms and conditions as they may deem advisable. After all the verbiage that we have in this Act, we wind up section 3 by saying that the'agreement may contain "such other terms and conditions as the parties may agree upon." If it is the intention of Parliament to restrict the agreement within certain bounds, the legislation should state so specifically. But it does not, because the Bill, gives them wide latitude. When this Bill is passed the world is before them and they can make smell terms as they deem fit. I think we should so frame the measure as to keep the bargain within the terms of the letter. It is not unreasonable to say, after two years of negotiation both in the Old Country and in Canada, that the Government have reached an understanding, not hurriedly but as a result of mature consideration, and we have the right to assume that everything they agreed upon is contained in that letter. We have been discussing this subject for some ten- days and if there has occurred to the ministers anything that is not in the letter and which should be in it, we have the right to know what it is. The Minister of Railways since eight o'clock has told us something in regard to the letter, about some mistake that might occur in connection with the hearing before the arbitrators, and that there must be power to go back of the arbitrators for ratification of the award if necessary. I think that that should be in the Bill and in the agreement based upon the Bill. It is certainly a matter of very 
substantial importance. If the award is. to be opened after the arbitration has been closed, there should be some statutory authority for that course. I am sure there would be very strenuous opposition on the part of the company to opening the award if it were satisfactory to them, and there should be no question about the authority for that action. If that proposition is in the letter and is not embodied in the Bill it could very well be argued afterwards that the letter was never intended to be acted upon, otherwise it would have been carried into the Bill.
I know of no argument that would appear stronger to a court. If the Minister of Railways lays any store by the proposition he made a moment ago he should put it in the Bill and it would free the legislation, so far as that particular point is concerned, from its present looseness.

The example cited by the Minister of the Interior is hardly similar to the clause under consideration. He told us that similar legislation had been enacted in 1903 in respect of aid to the Canadian Northern railway. In the statute cited by him the nature of the security that was to be given for the bonds, the part of the line which was to be mortgaged in security for the bonds, the lien and the rank of the lien, and everything else, was provided for. Nothing was left to the decision of the Governor in Council except the form of the trust deed. It was simply a matter of wording. In this Bill not only the wording ol the agreement is left to the Governor in Council, but the Bill says that the agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests comprised in the Grand Trunk system. So that the Governor in Council and the company may decide as to what will be transferred to the Government. Thus there is a vast difference between the legislation in 1903 and this Bill. While I am on this subject, I may ask the Minister of Railways to inform the committee who owns the Toronto Terminals Company. Is it part of the Grand Trunk Railway system and will it be transferred to the Government by the proposed agreement?
Mr. MBIiGHEN: I do not see much relation between the latter part of the hon. gentleman's speech and the first part of it.

My information is that the Toronto Terminals Company is owned by the Canadian Pacific railway and the

Grand Trunk jointly. So much for that. *The hon. member professes to find a vast difference between the instance that happened to be under my eye when I spoke, of Parliament giving the Governor in 'Council authority to insert terms and provisions in an agreement, and this instance. He says that in the agreement of 1903 there was stated in the Act the line that was to be mortgaged. Well, in this case, the whole subject matter is here, namely the properties of the Grand Trunk system. That is what we get, and we cannot alter the agreement in that respect. But a dozen or two dozen other provisions including sub-provisions must be embodied in the agreement. The only difference is that in 1903 the power granted the Governor in Council was infinitely more ample and much less circumscribed than this. And the 1903 case does not stand alone. I challenge the hon. gentleman to produce a single statute since then that does not include the same thing. I have the statute of 1908, passed by the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, granting if anything wider powers than were given in 1903. There is no use in argument if the hon. gentleman does not see that the authority is far more ample in those cases than in the one immediately under review. I am not finding fault with the statutes of those years. Similar statutes have been passed since the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier went out of power, and I doubt if there is a year since that time that similar statutes have not been passed.
It is the custom, and usually the power is much more ample than is asked for here. But hon. gentlemen' want something to complain of and they have kept this House all afternoon and evening professing themselves to be shocked because Parliament is asked that the Governor in Council be empowered to make such subsidiary and auxiliary terms and provisions as are consistent with the terms and provisions herein set cut and which are necessary to carry out these terms and provisions. Does my hon. friend imagine that there are terms in a trust deed that are not set out and provided for in the statute authorizing the trust deed? Did he ever see a trust deed? A trust deed is as thick through as your little finger. It is filled with terms and prolusions from beginning to end none of which is even mentioned or referred to in the authorizing statute.

speechtext:
There is no joke in that. I find that some of the applause behind the minister is the applause that welcomed remarks of the Minister of Railways the other night that were not worthy of any applause. I am now telling the minister that he asked me with a sneering smile whether I had ever seen a trust deed. I believe that any serious man in this House would take that as a sneer. There is nobody in this House who has had any training in business, and particularly a lawyer with a certain number of years (practice, but has seen a trust deed and knows what a trust deed is. I have seen a number of trust deeds. I know what they are and I will tell the minister that, notwithstanding his sneers, if he will patiently listen and look carefully into the matter, he will find a certain difference between the statute of 1903 and thp Bill now under consideration. That statute determines the rank of the mortgage on the property, determines that it shall be a mortgage on certain parts of the line, determines everything that is necessary to provide a first-class security for the bonds which are given up to the Government as security for its guarantee. Then, in so far as the form of the trust deed is concerned, it was left to the Governor in Council to deter-



mine, namely, the date of the guarantee as authorized, and the forms thereof; the forms and terms cf the mortgage and the time and the manner of issue. These are the conditions ordinarily contained in a trust deed. We determine when the obligations are going to be repaid, what shall be the rate of interest and various other clauses which the trust deed shall contain. In 1903 these matters were left to the Governor in Council. But the Governor in Council could not say that only one part of the line would be mortgaged. That was provided foT by statute. The Governor in Council could not say that there would be a second mortgage when the statute said that it should be a first mortgage. Everything essential to the security of the Government was absolutely provided for, leaving the wording and the ordinary clauses, which are the consequence of the trust deed, to be determined by the Governor in Council later on, so as not to relate in the statute everything contained in the trust deed which is as bulky as the minister has mentioned. But here in this Bill there is very much more than the form, the terms of the mortgage, the time of issue of the security, and the form and manner of the guarantee. Section 3 provides:
The said agreement shall contain provisions for the defining of the companies, properties and interests, comprised in the Grand Trunk system.
I contend, Sir, that before many courts of justice this can be interpreted as giving to the parties to the agreement the right to determine which companies or properties or interests shall be handed over by the company and shall become the property of the Government. If we have the right- to determine and define which companies, properties and interests are comprised in the Grand Trunk Railway system, the same right is given to determine and define which properties, companies or interests shall not form a part of that- system. It was in connection with this that I asked- the minister a question as to the terminals of the Grand Trunk in Toronto. Everybody was led to believe that the terminals in Toronto weic being built by the Grand Trunk and that the Canadian Pacific bad some arrangement with the Grand Trunk for using them as a union station. The House has not been told what interests are going to be defined as being transferred to the Government at the same time as the Grand Trunk Railway system. The minister 
appeared to think that it was irrelevant to the matter now under consideration. I maintain that if you provide in a section of the Bill now before the committee that the Government and the company shall have the right to define what companies, what properties, and interests are handed over with the Grand Trunk system, it is absolutely relevant to ask if the Toronto terminals are going to be transferred with the other properties and defined as forming part of the Grand Trunk railway system. The minister declares, "I do not know, but my information is that the Toronto terminals are jointly owned by the (Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk". We are desirous of knowing what will be defined as forming part of the Grand Trunk railway system and whether it would not be feasible to insert in the Bill a full definition, so that nothing will be left to haphazard in any agreements which may be entered into, which may have the result of eliminating part of that system. For example, a short time ago, I think it was yesterday, the point was discussed why the Grand Trunk Company had not. included in their financial statement for the last few years the receipts and the net earnings of the Canadian Transfer Company. I understand that that company, although it is owned by the Grand Trunk, is left as a separate concern, and the results of its operations were not shown in the Grand Trunk financial statement. I do not see that there would be any great difficulty in the Government so defining the Grand Trunk Railway system in this Bill that the public will know what it contains and nothing will be left for further definition by the Government and_the company in any subsequent agreement.

speechtext:
I do not remember any explanation at all. We were talking about it, it is true. I Teally think this question is of importance. We are told by the Government that they are relying entirely for information on. the Drayton-Acworth report. The Prime Minister in that cable in the blue-book which I have frequently quoted said that the Government should not take any steps in connection with acquiring the Grand Trunk property without some basis for every step they took. Now when we on this side of the House take that position, the Government say: We have the Drayton-Acworth report. Now the section of the Drayton-Acworth report which I read a few moments ago specifically says that five classes of stocks

will be satisfied or paid for by the division between them of a substantial part of $3,600,000 for the first seven years-from now on, say,-which amount could be added to as justified by conditions. Now that is not what is being done. The five stocks are not treated together. We are not going to pay the company merely a substantial portion of $3,600,000, but a great deal more, and when I ask why one of the stocks was taken out of the plan suggested by the Drayton-Acworth Commission, and 4 per cent interest guaranteed on it for all time to come, which alone gives the company more than is recommended in section 40, I can get no answer from the minister. I want to know for myself, and I think for the people I represent, what is the cause of this change of mind on the part of the Government. During the whole course of the negotiations up to the time the Prime Minister sent the cablegram to the High Commissioner in which he said the Government did not have any other information except the Drayton-Acworth report, and since, the Government have been relying entirely upon that report. Now they are travelling outside of that report and making a different bargain altogether, and when I ask what I regard as a serious question entitled to a proper explanation I am told by the Minister of the Interior that he said something about it this afternoon. Surely there must be some good reason why the Government departed from the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth report, and made a different proposal which is not supported by any report from anybody. We are told It is all right. You can ask as many questions as you like. But we do not get any explanation. There is no explanation for this, except that the Government is making a very much better bargain for the Grand Trunk than the Drayton-Acworth report recommends. For some mysterious [DOT]reason the Government finds it necessary to [DOT] call on the people of this country to pay more money to the owners of the Grand Trunk than was recommended by the Drayton-Acworth Commission of experts whom we appointed and paid to inform us what we should pay for this" road. The Government might as well be honest about it and admit at once that they are travelling entirely outside the Drayton-Acworth report and are acting on their own information and on their judgment. Do not let it be said any more that they are following the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth Commission,

because they are absolutely departing from the section I have read. It does not require any profound lawyer to see the difference, nor any profound knowledge of the manipulations of stocks and bonds. When we on this side of the House ask why things are not explainable we are told: " Oh, you are not familiar with the manipulation of stocks and bonds. If you were you would understand all about it." I believe I know as much about stocks and bonds as the ordinary citizen of this country. The farmers, the miners, the lumbermen, and the general public do not know very much about stocks and bonds, but they do know when they are making a fair deal and a good bargain. I submit to the minister that he is not making the bargain which the Drayton-Acworth Commission recommended, or we would not be in the position we are in to-day. I do not think the Grand Trunk would think of accepting the proposal of the Drayton-Acworth Commission, They played their cards very much better, and are getting a lot of money out of this country for which they are giving no adequate return. As the minister refuses to give me any answer I can only submit to the people of the country that the bargain the Government is now making is a new departure which finds no justification in the report which they quote as an authority.

speechtext: I understood the Minister of the Interior, in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Vien) to say that if certain stock was not handed in at a stated time an Order in Council would be passed declaring it to be the property of the Government. This procedure would appear to me to be in the nature of expropriation or confiscation. But the ministers who have charge of this Bill have all along stated that it was not the intention of the Government to confiscate any stock. In any event, how could an Order in Council passed by this Government be made effective as against people holding stock in a foreign country, England for instance? I understand that most of the shareholders reside in England, and if I mistake not the head office of the company is situated there. I am sure the hon. gentleman would not for a moment suggest that a Canadian company, merely by moving its head office out of Canada, could escape from the requirements of Canadian law. The stock of any Canadian company is subject to the jurisdiction of the proper constitutional authority in this country.
The railway company is subject to our jurisdiction if the company is incorporated by the Parliament of Canada. to have a certain number of shares vested in the Crown and a certain number still outstanding in the hands of shareholders. subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When this matter was under discussion the other night I ventured to ask the Minister of the Interior some questions about it. I pointed out to him that I had seen in the press that there are some 180,000 shareholders of the Grand Trunk holding preferred, common and guaranteed shares. These shareholders are not all in England; some are in Holland and other countries on the continent of Europe. It is very important that the Government should have some distinct understanding with the Grand Trunk that they would be in a position to deliver these shares when the Government was ready to hand over the guarantees provided for in this Bill. We have had no assurance so far from the .minister that the Grand Trunk has given any understanding of that kind to the Government. We learned from the minister the other day that he did not have any such understanding. What strikes me very forcibly is the difference between the opinion which my hon. friend expressed the other day when we discussed this same question and the opinion he expresses now. He now tells us that this Government can secure this stock by Order in Counoil, which is equivalent to confiscation. That is not what he said the other day when I raised the question. I pointed out to him that these shareholders might not surrender their stock and that part of the .property might stand in the name of shareholders located in different European countries. I also said that I did not think that the confiscation of these shares would be tolerated by the governments of the European countries in which these stockholders live. My hon. friend made this reply:
X am very glad to hear the sentiments in general that animate the hon. gentleman. X thoroughly agree with him that it would be entirely wrong on the part of this Parliament to pass a law which would confiscate the property of any person simply because we, or, indeed, some institution or commission appointed by us, declared that stock was of no value.
That was the opinion of my hon. friend two days ago. But to-night he informs the committee that if this difficulty does arise the Government will pass an Order in Council to practically confiscate the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, I do not change one hair's breadth from what I said on that occasion. The hon. gentleman was perfectly right then and I expressed my concurrence with the opinion that we should not, because we come to that conclusion ourselves, or because of some commission appointed by us, comes to the conclusion, arbitrarily declare that the stock is of no value. I have heard that suggested many times by more or less irresponsible hon. gentlemen but never by the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair). I took occasion to commend the sentiment that he expressed. We are not doing that now. We are not doing anything of the kind. If we are doing it now we did it in the Canadian Northern case, because we took exactly the same power, and exercised the same power in that case. There were some stocks in that case which were outstanding, which the parties did not bring in and we had the power to declare them our property and that power was exercised in regard to certain shares. There was no confiscation there and there will be none here. The Companies Act provides as respects ordinary Acts coming within that statute, that where there is a resolution of the shareholders passed in accordance with the provisions of that Act the other shareholders must abide by the terms of the resolution. There are similar clauses either in the chartering statute or in the by-laws passed under the chartering statute providing that the majority of the shareholders-possibly a. two-thirds majority-may bind the rest of the shareholders. We shall ask them to do so in this agreement and we shall ask them to legally execute this agreement [DOT] In that case, just as in similar cases, the minority shareholders are bound. Consequently there can be nothing in the way of an arbitrary deciding of values, nothing-far from it-in the way of confiscation, because what we do is by them agreed to in accordance with the provisions of the law defining what shall be an agreement on their part. I stated before, and I state again, we merely provide for the case of shares, perhaps in the hands of persons who never attended a meeting, but there is nothing done that the company does not agree to and that each shareholder does not agree to, in so far as his agreement is necessary by the law under which he holds his shares.

I cannot see that it is of very great importance; it may be that they can. Very frequently that is provided for by by-laws which the company themselves enact. But whether they can or not in any event the arguments of hon. gentlemen merely show that this is the only way to go about it. The object we have in. view is to establish a tribunal to determine the value, and having determined the value in a fair and square way, then to give the Governor in Council the power to carry out the exchange on that value. There is nothing confiscatory, nothing arbitrary, about it at all. The shareholders are given what the stock is worth. We are protected, because immediately the determination is made we have the power to declare that that stock is ours and the shareholder becomes entitled to his dividends on the voting certificates that are issued in exchange.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
We are dealing with a very important point of law and with property rights. The minister says that we can compel the transfer of these shares. We are taking for granted that many of these shareholders live beyond Canada. At all events, for the purpose of my argument, I am presuming that some of these shareholders live in England, Scotland and Ireland. Some of them perhaps live in France, and may refuse to transfer their shares. Let us say there is only one shareholder in France and that he has a thousand shares. He hears of this agreement but he holds on to his stock and refuses to transfer it. I ask the minister what can we do in this Parliament that would have any binding effect upon that citizen of France who owns a part of this property? So far as I have any knowledge we have no control over his person at all. This question is as old as the hills and it has always been enforced by the courts in England, in the event of the person who owned the property living in the country, that they would subject him to contempt, and would bring an action for specific performance. In that case, all the powers of the court can be exercised because the person lives in the country and is within the jurisdiction of Parliament and of the courts. But if the citizen who owned the property was beyond its jurisdiction, the court would be absolutely helpless-there would be nothing to do except agree with the man. Now here we are passing legislation which we say is going to expropriate the shares of a man who lives beyond the jurisdiction of this Parliament and beyond the jurisdiction of our courts, and we decree that an action shall be brought for specific performance. Our legislation enables the Minister of Railways, representing the Crown, to bring an action for specific performance; but we could not give any such authority as against the man beyond the confines of Canada. Our legislation would be absolutely without power; we could not authorize the courts to do that and we cannot do it ourselves. The principle is that we can exercise jurisdiction over the person of the man who owns property while he is within the jurisdiction of our courts and within the
jurisdiction of Parliament; but when he is beyond those confines and his property with him, we are absolutely hopeless, as I understand the law, except to have recourse to negotiation and agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The question the hon. member discusses is, of course, purely a legal one, and both he and I should apologize to the leader of the Opposition for taking up the time of the House upon it; but I will venture again to express, with all deference, what I myself regard, as the law on the point. He says that the owners of these shares are outside of Canada, they are domiciled in England, or in Holland, or in some other part of Europe; consequently, there is no way by which we can enforce a surrender of the shares. He is quite right, I think, in saying that we have no remedy as against the owner of the shares-that is, no remedy, as we call it, in persona. But we have a remedy in this, that what we wish to attach to ourselves, and release from the shareholder, is Canadian property.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The share is not Canadian property.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Oh yes, because it is
a share of a Canadian company.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
We do not agree in that. I submit that when a share is issued and the stock paid for and passed to the person concerned, it is as much his property as a twenty-pound note.
Mr. MEIGH'EN: Certainly it is his property; that is to say, he is the owner of it, but it is a Canadian property. For example, were he the owner of a piece of land along the right of way of a railway that we were projecting, the property would be Canadian property owned by this man who is over in Holland. But the hon. member would scarcely argue that in such a case we could not have the right of way because we could not expropriate property owned by a man in Holland. It is just the same here only that the property is a share certificate issued by a Canadian
10 p.m. company and consequently as a property is subject to the jurisdiction of Canadian laws. We exercise that jurisdiction in rem by saying: We may declare that that voting certificate of a Canadian company is our property, and we pay to the man in Holland or in England such sum for it as the award of the board of arbitration may warrant.

speechtext:
There is a difference, Mr. Chairman, between real estate and personal property. I submit that the shares of a

company are either real estate or personal property. If they are personal property, there is an axiom of law which says that personal property follows the person- mobilia sequuntur personam. I fancy that that rule applies to property of this kind; it applies to shares which are personal property.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Assuming that the
share certificates are personal property, that is, that the proprietary ownership of the company is personal property-assuming that-the property is, nevertheless, Canadian personal property. What represents it may be held corporeally over in Holland, but the stuff is here. Suppose there is a personal property here, say some furniture, and the bill of sale or whatever may represent it is over in Holland; that personal property here is subject to the jurisdiction of the proper legislature in this country. Similarly, the ownership of the share, that personal property represented by the certificate is subject to our jurisdiction though the man who holds the paper representing the ownership of that property is in Holland. The share certificates of a Canadian company are subject to Canadian jurisdiction. I venture to think that the bon. member, with the training that he has had and the predisposition that he has in the matter of safeguarding Canadian autonomy and Canadian rights, would be about the last to argue that either the Canadian Federal Parliament or a Canadian Provincial Parliament should be powerless with regard to the disposition of property in a Canadian company.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
A large amount of revenue is derived by the Grand Trunk system through the operation on its lines of Pullman sleeping cars. Whether the Pullman people are shareholders in the Grand Trunk or whether they get their profits on a mileage basis or otherwise, certainly a proportion of the earnings of the road are required to pay them for the operation of these cars. I understand that the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific own and operate their own sleeping cars, but the Grand Trunk Railway Company operate Pullman cars which are the property of a company in the United States. These cars are operated over all the lines of the Grand Trunk, and I believe that fares are collected upon them by the servants of the Pullman Company, though I arq not sure as to that. It would be interesting to the committee to have a statement as to what arrangement there is

between the Grand Trunk and the Pullman people; how the revenues derived from the operation of these cars are distributed, and how long the arrangement has been in existence. If we know exactly how these revenues are disposed of, complications may be avoided later.

speechtext:
Are we
to understand that the hon. Minister of Railways, having answered the question put by the hon. member from Brantford in the manner he did, holds that no member of this House has the right to protest against the course of the Government, particularly the hon. Minister of Railways, against his inefficiency, his lack of capacity, I would even say his lack of knowledge as to the subject matter of this discussion. That is what I am coming to.
I stated that the hon. Minister of Railways was unable at this stage to give the necessary explanations which we have the right to expect from him. Even the friends of the Government, hi.s own followers, think they are themselves fairly and conscientiously entitled to call upon him to give those explanations.
I was saying a moment ago that friends of the Government, partisan newspapers, the Gazette and the Star, in Montreal, as well as their confederates, protest against the taking over of that railway by the Government on account of the large increase in the public debt which it will entail, and that, under such circumstances, the Government should not proceed any further nor set public opinion at defiance. What happened in the province of Quebec, in 1914, when certain charges were made against the Government of that time by Messrs. Beck, McNab and Nichol, who were then managers of a newspaper in Montreal? When those accusations were levelled at the Government charging them with embezzlement, they brought the accusers before the bar of the House and compelled them to prove their charges.
Should not the Government do likewise to-day and compel the editors of those newspapers to substantiate the charges set forth or implied in the editorials which we have read?
It would be interesting to get explanations upon that print at the bar of this House from Lord Atholstan and hon. Senator White, as well as from other friends of the Government who caused their advent to power in 1911 and 19i7; it would also be interesting to peep behind the scenes and to get the names of all those 'concerned, of all the friends of the Government who are so insistent upon the passing of this measure as soon as possible.
If the Government do not dare to let us know, it is because they are afraid those charges are "well founded, they are fearful of their judgment and of public opinion.

speechtext: If the liabilities of the company are not to be increased by the amount of the new stock, we must admit either that the new stock should be looked upon as having no value, except in so far as title in the actual shareholders is concerned, or else we must recognize that the old stock which will be handed to the Government will cease to have its value. If the new stock is a liability against the company, and if the old stock also remains a liability against the company, we cannot escape the conclusion that the liabilities of the company are increased by the amount of the new stock.

speechtext: The old stock is no liability against the company; it appears as a book-keeping entry on the liability side, but the stock of the company is not a liability of the company in the sense that it must pay anything. As long as the hon. gentleman knows what is being done, it matters^ very little about the mere charging of it. The fact of the matter is that the owners of all these stocks, the three preference and common, will get instead of their shares whatever value the arbitrators determine they are worth, and they get that value in the shape of Government-guaranteed stock. That is all there is to it.

I think we established last night, and even before, that the Government on account of committing itself to $216,000,000 and over in this transaction has a direct interest in this company and that forever in the future it will have to back up the company should that backing be needed, and that the concern will practically belong to the Government when this transaction is consummated. practically it will, because 'the Government will have to back it up whenever it is necessary to do so. If this were a transaction between two railway companies it would be quite clear that the Bill is loading up the concern with a lot of watered stock. You are going to take $180,000,000 of old stock and buy it up at a reduced price, let us hope, and issue new stock for it. They both represent the same thing, and if you leave both stocks afloat, then you are watering the stock in a huge way. If it were5 simply a transaction between two railway companies it could not be allowed. I do not think it makes any difference, because when the Government gets the stock, whether they cancel it or put in the safe, the result is the

same. If they cancelled it, of course, that would be the end of it, and it would also be practically the end- of it if they put it in the safe, for there is no reasonable probability that it would pay a dividend, and if it did the Government would get the dividend.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If it were cancelled there would have to be some means of issuing new common stock to give the voting power to the company.

speechtext: It is quite evident that there are two sets of stock representing the same property. You are going to buy $180,000,000 of preference "and common stock by issuing another stock. If you let them both stand you are loading up the company with watered stock, and if it were a transaction between two companies it could not be done. But practically speaking, this stock that is called in, whether cancelled or not, does not really amount to anything in the result. It is a mere matter of accounting. It may stand as a liability. If it ever earns dividends the Government, being the owners of the stock, will get the dividends. I do not think we need be alarmed about that aspect of the question.

speechtext: Clause 4 strikes me as being the most objectionable clause in the whole Bill. The Government represented to the House and the committee that the Grand Trunk Company had to come to them for assistance, and that it was necessary to introduce this Bill to save the company and continue the operations of these railways. If this Bill were not introduced, it was said, there would be a financial collapse of the Grand Trunk. Now, I submit that it was not necessary for the Government to take $60,000,000 of common stock, largely watered, and place their stamp on it, making it worth four .per cent perpetually. Why was it done? No minister has given the House an intelligent reason for that action. It was not done in order to get the contract, because the Government had ample means of forcing the contract. The Grand Trunk Company was indebted to the Government. They were unable to implement their guarantee in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Government could have put them into liquidation if it chose. The Government cannot therefore claim that they were forced to guarantee $60,000,000 of worthless stock and put their "stamp on it, making it perpetual bonds at the rate of four per cent. I do not say the stock was altogether watered, 'but we know that it was largely so.

speechtext:
When this stock was selling a few weeks ago in London at 50, why should the Government step in and guarantee it at the rate of four per cent perpetually? What is the reason that this should be done? My principal objection to this clause is that we are involving the country in a perpetual guarantee for $60,000,000 of this stock. It is quite true that it had the guarantee of the Grand Trunk, but it had no guarantee that gave it the position of bonds. It had not paid any dividends for the last two years because dividends were not earned by the company. If the company continued to fail to earn dividends the stock with the Grand Trunk guarantee would not be worth any more in tiie market than it was worth at that date.
My hon. friend has constantly impressed upon the House the Drayton-Acworth report, and we have been told repeatedly by him that the Government is proceeding on the recommendations made in that report. We find at page 65 of the report the following statement:
We regard the entire share capital of the company as being intrinsically of hut small value at the present time. On the basis of present value of maintainable income the fair compensation would be very small.
In the face of thaf opinion my hon. friend undertakes to give the guarantee of the country to a stock which he admits himself is only worth 50 cents on the dollar, and he proposes to make it worth 80 or 90. On that question of value my hon. friend made a statement this afternoon that four per cents were only worth 721 in the London market. I took occasion subsequently to look at some of the London papers to see whether that statement was correct or not. I found the following in a paper called "Canada" dated September 20, 1919: Canadian Finances.
Among the Canadian securities business has been fairly brisk. The gilt-edged issues of the Dominion have been maintained. The 4J per cents hold at 95 and the fours at 78. The 3$ per cents are steady at 71.
My hon. friend told us this afternoon that 4 per cents were holding at about 721 whereas the London papers say they are holding steadily at 78. There is a considerable difference between the statement of the Minister of the Interior and the statements which I find in the London papers. We can argue then that this 4 per cent guarantee given by the Government makes this stock worth 78 in the London market, and if that is so in the case of $60,000,000 worth of stock, we are incurring a very heavy liability amounting to many



millions of dollars which we are placing on the backs of the people unnecessarily. It should not be dione. Therefore, I propose an amendment. The section reads:
As part of the consideration for such acquisition, the Government may agree to guarantee the payment of:-
(a) dividends payable half-yearly, at 4 per cent per annum, upon the present guaranteed stock.
I move:
That section 4 be amended by striking therefrom subclause (a).

Because the rate is
higher. I do not want the hon. gentleman to get unnecessarily into a hole and he should not be too positive. If you take a low rate of interest, below the normal rate, below the rate that brings the stock to par, money is worth about 5i per cent, and a Canadian bond issue is worth 721, that means that a 51 per cent bond will sell at 100. Take another bond issue at a lower rate, say 4, or 3 per cent, the longer that bond issue the less it is worth; the shorter the bond issue the more it is worth. If it is within a year of maturity it is worth nearly par. But if you have a 7 per cent bond issue, the longer it has to run the more it is worth, and the shortor it has to run the less it is worth.	_
It is only because the hon. gentleman did not think the matter out that ne ventured to contradict what I said. I do not know what the hon. gentleman was quoting, but it is very probably a bond issue and if it is anything at all but a perpetual bond it has likely only a short time to run.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I may tell the
minister that the information is not given in the quotation but I would be glad to give it to him.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It is likely of the character I have mentioned, because if the hon. gentleman will take his pencil and figure out if a 5} per cent is worth 100-and mind you, you have to create a tremendous organization and carry out a great campaign indeed to get it sold at that figure, but suppose it is really worth 100 in the market -then a 4 per cent will be worth 72 and a fraction just as I said this afternoon. If the bond is of short date it will be worth more, but we are giving our perpetual security here and our perpetual security, issued at four per cent, could not sell at more, even if it were a direct security, than 72 and a fraction. But, it is indirect and could not be worth more than 68 or 69.' The other issue was sold at I think, about 55. The difference is appreciation, it is true, but there is no way of avoiding it because any payment at all on the stock must be first applied on that bond issue, because they have priority [DOT]-priority as to principal in the event of liquidation, and priority as to interest all the time as a charge against revenue. Now that being so, once it is agreed that $2,500,-

000 shall be paid for the whole five years on guaranteed, the three preference stocks, and common, that means that the guaranteed stock must get the whole thing; it could not be avoided. But we get something in return, we get from the holders of these guaranteed stocks a surrender of their voting power. Why, it is only three or four hours since we were charged by an hon. member opposite with confiscation-that was the complaint against the Government in connection with this transaction. I defended the measure by saying that the impression of the guarantee of the Government caused an appreciation in the value which the shareholders got in lieu of the surrender of the voting power, so that taking it all in all it was fair and no more than fair. The point the hon. gentleman raises was fully considered, the difficulty he has intimated was carefully reviewed, but as we had undertaken to pay $2,500,000-an offer which they turned aside and refused for a year and-a-half-and as the owners of these bonds had to get all the first money, and as we were, in making that offer, carrying out strictly the Drayton-Acworth report, there was no way of avoiding that appreciation. We would have preferred not to do anything to appreciate the value of anything that we do not get consideration for, but we do not suffer directly or indirectly -it is only a fair payment made in accordance with the Drayton-Acworth report.

speechtext:
I have been over this point so often that I must apologize for allucjing to it again, but I must make an observation or two in reply to what the hon. gentleman has just said. There are a few facts here which we should clearly bear in mind. In the first place, it is evident, and has been stated repeatedly, that this guaranteed stock was quoted on the London Stock Exchange a short time ago at forty-five. I gave a quotation of forty-eight on the 18th day of September, and it was stated that there had been a " burst," to use a stock market expression, which had advanced it to that point. Now, if any private individual had wanted that stock he would have gone about it in a simple way. He would have gone to the holders and made them a public offer through brokers and said: " This stock is worth forty-five and we are willing to give you something more than that figure. We will be liberal and give you something even higher than that, something over the market value, as an inducement to sell." The hon. gentleman might very fairly say:
94 i
" But they will not sell." Very well, all the Government had to do was to leave the stock with them and say: " We do not want to confiscate your stock. We offered you something over the market value, we offered you a premium. If you do not want to sell it, all right; keep it and we will protect you in your present rights. Whatever interest, whatever dividend, is earned on that stock you will get and if no dividend is earned you will not get it." When I raised that point the hon. gentleman said-and I am sorry I have to repeat the same argument,-" In that case there could not be a merger of the various interests," He was entirely wrong, as I pointed out at the time. All these companies have subsidiary organizations. Why, the Grand Trunk Pacific, as he knows, is a separate company from the Grand Trunk, and there has to be a separate accounting for its earnings. He knows that the Central Vermont, with which we are dealing, is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk and there has to be a separate account kept of its earnings. It is a common thing in the history of railroading to keep account of the earnings of one branch of the railway separate from another. There is nothing remarkable about it. The Minister of Railways to-day has an agreement with the Government of New Brunswick, in connection with the national system of railroads, under which a certain percentage of the earnings is taken for the provincial government and a certain percentage for the Dominion Government. Therefore the argument that under the arrangement I propose, you could not create a merger, is entirely wrong. There is nothing in that argument-any railroad man in the world would tell you that, There may be some little difficulty in doing it, but it is a common thing in the history of railroading to keep separate accounts for different branches or different-sections of a road. Now if the owners of that stock were not content to sell it, were not content to take the market value and even take a handsome premium on the' market value, it would have been the easiest thing in the world to have said, "All right, keep the stock, and if there are any earnings coming to you, you will get them." That would have been a fair' businesslike proposal and that is what would have been done if it had been a transaction between private individuals. Now we come to the question of the value of the stock. I have said that in my judgment-not at the moment but when financial matters are readjusted-the stock on which we impress

the guarantee of the Government of Canada will be advanced from 45 to 85 or 90. There is at present a financial depression and I do not say that you could sell it for 90 to-day; but I believe 1 am fairly within the mark, and gentlemen familiar with London financial affairs will say, that at no distant day when things get settled down, that stock will be worth 85 or 90. But suppose it is not going to be worth that? Suppose it is only going to be worth about 70? The difference between 45 and 70 is 25 points. Twenty-five points on $60,000,000 means a clear sheer waste of the public money of the Dominion of $15,000,000. There is no escaipe from that; it is absolutely beyond argument. If any argument could be put up against that 1 have yet to hear it. The merger argument is answered; my hon. friend must see that was wrong. "Ah," he says, "but there is the voting power." That implies that we were dependent upon the Grand Trunk people to get the voting power. That is not the situation. The Grand Trunk Company is-I do not want to say a bankrupt company, that is a harsh phrase-in default with the Government, and the Government * are not bound to be dictated to by the company. The Government are 'bound to be fair to the Grand Trunk and then say, '-1i you are not content with a fair arrangement all we can do is to have you go into -the hands of a receiver," and where would their voting power be then? Bo that on every point it seems to me this is a most wasteful and improvident transaction. In my judgment it is clearly a sheer waste of at least twenty-five or thirty millions of dollars of the money of the people of Canada; and even accepting the statement of the hon. gentleman himself it is a sheer waste of at least $15,000,000 of the money of the Dominion, no penny of which was necessary to be paid.
