How would the offer be made? How would he reach the hundred thousand shareholders? In the next place, presuming that we reached the alternative, that they did not take it, and we left them with their shares, have they not the voting power? They are part proprietors. In the first announcement that went out as to the tvans-

action that was arranged certain newspapers got the idea that just that thing was done. The Toronto Globe, fearing that the guaranteed stock was being left in the hands of these tens of thousands of people with whom we were going into partnership in the running of the Grand Trunk, published a denunciatory article. So did a western paper. But it was not done The hon. gentleman thinks it would be all right for the Government of Canada to share proprietorship of the road with thousands upon thousands of shareholders over in England; to share control with them; to be compellable to send them notices of meetings and all that before we could do anything in connection with the road. A more absurd position could scarcely be conceived.
Now, I repeat with all the emphasis in my power that merger is absolutely impossible if we have to account to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk. It may be possible with a single road, because that is not merger at all; that is not what merger means. For example, only part of the stock of the Duluth and Western is owned by the Canadian Northern system, of which we own the stock; consequently .there has to be a separate accounting of the operations of the Duluth and Western. But that is an easy matter; that is just one single little line. We are not closing off anything in connection with it; we are operating it just like any other, and of course, we are doing justice to the minority shareholders of that line. The Central Vermont is in virtually the same position in respect of the Grand Trunk; it is one single line and the Grand Trunk accounts to the minority shareholders of that line-there' is no difficulty there. But here is a whole system, the whole Grand Trunk system. It is true that we can keep account of its operations; that is not the difficulty, and I have never pointed that out as a difficulty. The difficulty is this: Suppose we decided that it was in the interests of economy, now that we are owners of the Grand Trunk, to close the line between Toronto and Ottawa, would we be able to do it? We find at the end of the year that we have no four per cent for the guaranteed stockholders, and they ask us : " How is this?" "Well," we tell them, "we did not earn it. Here are the 'accounts.; we did not earn it on your system." But they say:: "You closed off that line and you diverted all its earnings into the Canadian Northern, the competitor of the Grand Trunk between Ottawa and Toronto. It is very easy for you to tell us that you have no

dividends for us when you closed off our line in order that your other lines might pay better." That is one illustration. That is what merger means; that is the advantage of merger-and all that we throw away, deny ourselves the right to. do, if we are under an accounting obligation to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk. Nothing could be clearer than that. It is very different when you start to merge a system. The merging of a system means the lopping off if lines where the whole combined system can be made to pay better as a result; it is the utilization of the facilities of one for the benefit of the other. That is impossible if you must fairly account to the shareholders of the system merged.

: Well, keeping the accounts is all that is necessary in order to render to the stockholders the dividends that they earn. My hon. friend introduces into the matter the Toronto Globe article. It would have been just as appropriate if I had introduced the interesting articles from the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Star, but if I did so my hon. friend would say that my remarks were not to the point. I have not done it, but my hon. friend drags in the Toronto Globe and says that it/ has said something about how the Grand Trunk might be treated. I am not responsible for the Toronto Globe; I propose to discuss this question simply and solely as a business proposition and on its merits.
When the hon. gentleman speaks of all these difficulties of accounting I say that his argument is absolutely unwarranted. Every large railway concern in Canada has its subsidiary companies; and while I do not say that there is no difficulty, I do say that the difficulty is easily overcome. I again remind my hon. friend that sitting beside him is the Minister of Railways, who is pledged to render a separate accounting of the St. John Valley railway, taking for the Government of Canada only a cerain percentage and giving a certain percentage to the stockholders, who are
the Government of New Brunswick. If it is possible to do it in that case, it is possible to do it in a larger way; that is plain.
The hon. gentleman talks about injustice being done the shareholders. Surely there can be no injustice if you offer these people the market price and more than the market price. If they do not want it, and you say: "Well, gentlemen, we leave it in your hands and we will protect your interests," I cannot see any injustice in that. If the Grand Trunk shareholders are unreasonable; if they demand things which are utterly unfair and unjust, the hon. member has his remedy. We are the creditors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and upon application the Grand Trunk Railway Company'can be put in the hands-of a receiver just as easily as the Grand' Trunk Pacific was put in the hands of a receiver. That done, what becomes of alii this voting power?. Why do we need to make sacrifices to get the voting power, when we could get it by the other method? I am not advising that the Grand Trunk be puit in the hands of a receiver, but I say that it is a perfectly open coures for us. If the Grand Trunk people were not willing to be fair; if they would not receive a generous and fair offer in the right spirit, then we would be justified in putting the road in the hands of a receiver.

As to this talk of $ 15,000,000 or $20,000,000 being wasted, I want to tell him that if it was $120,000,000 that was necessary to be spent to keep up the good name of Canada, that would not be waste from my point of View. I want to appeal further to my hon. friend. I heard with the greatest pleasure his expression of a belief which was in absolute accord with the belief which I myself had expressed in a session not long ago that in time this great country will be big enough to sustain these roads. He defended, and I sympathized with him in his defence, what the Government did of which he was a member. I share with him absolutely that faith in the future of Canada, but I should lose that faith if I allowed myself to descend to this niggling method of bargaining with those who very often are widows and need their dividends to keep them going. Investments made on the good faith of our country require that we should approach them in a mood of justice, yes, of justice, but of fairness, and I would even add of generosity.

With nearly everything my hon. friend has said I can cordially agree, but let us come down from the clouds and be practical. The English business man, especially the Englishman in the London market, is a very practical person, and the widows and orphans who have bought this stock in by-gone years have probably passed away. The stock, I venture to say, in the past six months has fallen largely into the hands of some of those Jews in London, whom my hon. friend would not have us take as models to follow in bargaining. Therefore, I think that the $15,000,000 or $20,000,000, or possibly $25,000,000, of money which is going to be wasted in this ease will not go into the hands of

the widows and orphans, but into the hands of the London speculators who have been buying this stock at low market rates and waiting for the Government of Canada to put the stamp of the Government guarantee upon it, which will give them all this money.
There is one other point I wish to make. My hon. friend speaks of a niggling proposal. My suggestion was that we should not tie these people down to the market value of the stock, though there would be no injustice in that. The Englishman does not expect any "baby act" in the average business transaction. He does not expect more than the market value in anything. My proposal was that we should offer these people five or ten points above the market value. What would that mean? It would mean a clean gift of $6,000,000 of the people's money over and above what the market value demanded, and my hon. friend says that is a niggling policy.

It should be added in justice to the stockholders that it is altogether unfair, altogether erroneous, and I think worse, to allege that the stock has changed hands as the result of anything that has gone on in this country. Stock in Great Britain is bought for purposes of investment, and not for purposes of exchange on the stock market. Only such stock goes on the market as somebody has to sell as occasion demands. I have endeavoured to find out the amount that has changed hands, and it is very, very small. There necessarily are quotations because some little amount reaches the market, but the stock is held in the main just where it has been held, in some cases for the last ten, twenty, thirty and even forty years. That is the information from the directors of the company. The percentage that changes hands is almost negligible, and the percentage that has changed hands recently, I venture to say, and will confirm it later, is practically negligible. All this impression sought to be made by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) and others that there is stock jobbing by some persons near the Govern-

ment to any ^extent whatever is a false impression, an unworthy impression, and I am sorry my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is associated with it.

speechtext:
In view of the
persistency of my hon. friend (Mr. Meigh-en) in stating that the Canadian Pacific is behind any opposition to this legislation,
I should like to call his attention to a speech made by the president of that company, Mr. Beatty, in the presence of Lord Shaughnessy and all the great millionaires , of .the city of Montreal at the opening of the Victory Loan campaign in this city last week. After Sir Henry Drayton had spoken on the Victory Loan, Mr. Beatty stated that the Canadian Pacific railway had absolutely nothing to do with the opposition to this legislation, and I accept his word. He stated that the Canadian Pacific could not buy the Grand Trunk railway without the permission of the Government, and in any case they did not want it, because it would mean that in many places they would be simply paralleling their own lines, and in
a way setting up an opposition to themselves. Speaking rather sarcastically of the Drayton-Acworth report Mr. Beatty expressed his surprise that a great lawyer like Sir Henry Drayton had produced no better arguments in his report. He then went on to say that they were not there to discuss railway matters but the Victory Loan, and to show that the Canadian Pacific wanted to help the country meet its obligations he announced that that company was going to take $20,000,000 of bonds; which they have done.
When the Government refuses to pay any attention to the president of the Canadian Pacific I aim bound to ask myself if there are not outside interests behind this transaction. It is said that t)he Canadian- Pacific Railway Company was anxious that the receiver should be appointed, but the ministers have given no proof in support of this assertion. Does it not -appear to you, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of the Interior should realize that one receiver would be quite competent to deal with the whole system? Of course, he does, but he endeavours to make us believe, if we were so credulous, that fifty or seventy-five receivers, or as many as there -are lines, are necessary. He said also that it would be impossible to keep the operating accounts of these several lines. Well, if that be so, it only proves that- his employers are incapable, and should be summarily dismissed. Now, Mr. Chairman, I desire to have it distinctly understood that the -Canadian Pacific Railway Company exercises no influence on me, and so far as the. ownership of Canadian railways is concerned, I may say that when the Government undertook to- acquire the Canadian Northern, I stated that I would be in favour of public ownership on condition that all the railways were acquired at the same time and operated under government control. I think that that would have been infinitely better than acquiring the railways piecemeal. In regard to the Canadian Northern stock, I expressed the opinion that the Government should buy the majority of the stock. Instead of doing that, they referred to arbitrators the question of the value of this stock. The result was that the -country had to pay $10,800,000 for stock which was valueless. And they are proposing the same thing in this case. The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is well acquainted with transactions of this kind, and he knows very well that this Bill is so drawn as to afford opportunities of speculation to- those who are behind this transaction. It is framed in such a

way as to give the greatest benefit to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk. It is for this reason that the Government have encountered opposition from the Board of Trade of Montreal, who decided that there was nothing further to be done in the matter since the Government was determined to put this legislation through. The delegation that waited upon the Government is now before the Senate, and I trust its representations will be more successful. I hope that the Senate at the proper time will deal with the Bill in such an effective way as to show to the members in this House who are bound to suipiport it here that it is a-n ill-considered measure.
